subtopic: CONGRATULATIONS TO CANADIAN DOWNHILL SKI TEAM FOR SUCCESS IN WORLD CUP-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the current debate over the use of motions under Standing Order 43, and the limitations extending to these motions which occasionally prevent matters of urgent national importance being brought to the attention of this House, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin):
That this House direct the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization to immediately review the provisions of Standing Order 43 which now apparently prevents a motion being brought to the attention of this House congratulating the Canadian downhill ski team on their outstanding performance in the opening race of the World Cup, and exhorting them to greater success for the glory of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to move a motion, under Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
As it is essential that this country overcomes the $12.5 billion a year trade deficit which we have in fully manufactured goods, and as this can only be done if we greatly increase our sales effort abroad and let far more people in the world market know what this country has to offer, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Victoria-Haliburton (Mr. Scott):
That this government allow producers to write off 200 per cent of all expenses connected with making sales trips abroad, displaying their products at foreign trade fairs, and any other expenses incurred in sales promotion in the export market in excess of those made in the base year, the year before the plan goes into operation.

subsubtopic: MONITORING OF AND COMPENSATION FOR WORKERS EXPOSED TO ASBESTOS HAZARDS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, under the provisions of Standing Order 43-a matter connected with the news that a number of people who were employed in a Second World War Defence Research Board plant which processed asbestos-filled gas masks have begun having problems associated with exposure to asbestos. An unusually large proportion of these people have died of lung diseases associated with asbestos exposure, and the others are undoubtedly at risk.
In the light of this situation and the government's liability in these cases, I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Rae):
That the government at once set up procedures to identify all the employees of wartime defence plants who may be similarly at risk from asbestos exposure, arrange to have them monitored for the appearance of related problems, and compensate them adequately for the suffering involved. This compensation should, of course, include the widows and families of those who have already died from such problems.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: LABOUR FORCE FIGURES PUBLISHED BY STATISTICS CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. Statistics Canada has now confirmed what we have been trying to tell the hon. gentleman for some considerable time, namely, that the hidden jobless rate in this country is much greater than we have been led to believe and substantially more than the figures released every month by Statistics Canada.
Will the minister, as a matter of course, when he releases or responds to the monthly labour force surveys by Statistics Canada, indicate the extent of this hidden unemployment; or, at the very least, since this data is to be computed on a regular basis, will he make known to us the number of people registered at Manpower offices across the country, a figure which is always substantially more than that given in the official labour force survey, so that we may have a true picture of exactly how serious the situation is?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: LABOUR FORCE FIGURES PUBLISHED BY STATISTICS CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Statistics Canada did conduct, in March of this year, an experimental project to determine whether this method of survey could be used. The result was that they felt it was experimental, it was not very solidly based, and they have informed me that the most solid and objective measure of unemployment is the number of those who are without work and who are actively looking for work. Countries which use the household survey method accept that this is, in fact, the best and most honest basis of determining the measure of unemployment.
The provisos expressed by Statistics Canada with regard to the difficulty of obtaining unambiguous and meaningful estimates of the number of people who want work and who are not actively seeking employment are likely to be ignored. They pointed this out in their report, to be fair to StatsCan, and in
Oral Questions
no way suggested that this number should be made available in addition to the others. We have indicated, in our labour force survey figures, the kind of information the hon. member is looking for. 1 believe the figure in November was something like 63,000.

subsubtopic: LABOUR FORCE FIGURES PUBLISHED BY STATISTICS CANADA
speechtext:
1 asked this question with respect to the March survey in a question I placed on the order paper last June. It is rather interesting that the question was replied to in the House on October 10. At that time I was told that the result of the survey would be released and that they would give consideration to having this additional data on a regular basis. The minister tends to discredit this new data, so I ask whether he feels the same way about his own Manpower offices across the country, because according to the data in March when StatsCan was reporting 1,045,000 Canadians out of work, his offices across the country indicated there were 1,389,000 Canadians registered as looking for jobs.
I ask the minister, so that we can get a reasonable assessment of the situation, whether he could release monthly the number of registered Canadians with the labour force survey at Manpower offices so that we can get the true picture. If not, is he going to discredit his own Manpower figures; or what is the situation?

subsubtopic: LABOUR FORCE FIGURES PUBLISHED BY STATISTICS CANADA
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, it is not a question of discrediting Manpower figures. Many people who are registered at Manpower offices are already at work. Some of those who have registered at Manpower offices have already found work. So if we were trying to misinform the Canadian public, that would be one of the ways to go about it.
StatsCan has the officials, the experts and the professionals to do all of the labour force surveys. They are very good at their jobs. They have indicated that they are trying an experimental approach in March which, as they have said, is fraught with difficulties, fraught with errors, and it would be inappropriate to add those figures to the level of unemployed. We have indicated that to the best of our knowledge, given the information we get from StatsCan, the figure of-"discouraged workers", at the highest, is something like 63,000-and that information is made public.

subsubtopic: LABOUR FORCE FIGURES PUBLISHED BY STATISTICS CANADA
speechtext:
Perhaps I can approach it this way. I checked with my own province where we have, I suppose, more discouraged job seekers than anywhere else in Canada because of the chronic, long-term nature of unemployment. 1 find that in Newfoundland, for the month of November, while StatsCan was reporting 31,000 officially unemployed, there were 62,000 registered at Manpower offices as looking for jobs. I submit to the minister that those 62,000 people were without jobs: certainly, they would not be registered and looking for jobs in a province where the official rate of unemployment is considerably higher than other provinces.
Let me frame my question by asking the minister the following: in view of the fact that Manpower training and job-creation programs are based on official labour force sur-

veys from StatsCan, and in view of the fact that StatsCan, by their own admission, now admit to the inadequacy of labour force surveys based on the hidden jobless-the people who, out of sheer frustration, have given up looking for a job-will the minister now reassess the data that he uses to measure the extent of Manpower training programs and make-work programs?

subsubtopic: LABOUR FORCE FIGURES PUBLISHED BY STATISTICS CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his preamble, the hon. member has gone into four or five different areas. I have indicated to him that mere registration at a Manpower office does not indicate that an individual is unemployed. Many are looking for better employment, some are looking for jobs that would be easier for them physically, and others feel they are underemployed and would like to know, when jobs come up, that they will be called. So it would be misleading and inappropriate to use the numbers registered at Manpower offices.
I give full marks to StatsCan for trying constantly, through one method or another, to give us accurate statistics. They have indicated to us, and I quote them, that "the most solid and objective measure of the numbers of unemployed is indicated by those without work and who are actively looking for work." Given those particular statistics, they have a relative basis right across the country, so that no one is left out. As a matter of fact, the hon. member should know that his own province, in Canada works projects, ranks fourth in the gross amount of money that is received. subsubtopic: CRITICISM OF GOVERNMENT TRAINING PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Employment and Immigration: it relates to a report on the training of skilled, blue collar workers prepared for the Department of Employment and Immigration by Robertson, Nickerson Group Associates Limited.
Will the minister tell the House whether he agrees with the report's conclusions that the federal government has failed to supply leadership, that government training programs "need a massive overhaul", and that "the opportunity for high level young Canadians to get into a skilled trade is so non-existent that this situation can be described as disgraceful"? If the minister does agree with this assessment, can he tell the House what action he proposes to take, as minister, to rectify the situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: CRITICISM OF GOVERNMENT TRAINING PROGRAMS
speechtext:
I always feel that individuals who are writing reports and come to a particular conclusion use words that are bound to catch the eye and are bound to be printed. The fact is that we have tripled the amount of money we are making available under the apprenticeship program, just as one indicator.
[Mr. McGrath.)
We have just completed ten agreements, one with each of the provinces, under the Adult Occupational Training Act. The hon. member spoke about federal government programs. With respect, I should like to indicate that education is a field solely within the jurisdiction of the provinces. In fact we are buying places in the provinces for the kind of training they want. I have indicated in the House and in other places that, frankly, I am dissatisfied with the fact, having done a study in southwestern Ontario primarily, that 75 per cent of the high skilled jobs were filled by immigration rather than on the job training. I am trying to encourage industry, through the shifting of funding to industry, to play a larger role in on the job training and to make more funds available to provide that opportunity for the young people in the country. I think it is a better approach than relying on immigration to fill these jobs.

subsubtopic: CRITICISM OF GOVERNMENT TRAINING PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the report is eye-catching in its conclusions. It points out the reason such a high percentage of skilled blue collar workers have come to Canada is that it was promoted by the federal government and not by industry because of the lack of skilled labour available for blue collar industrial trades. The report points out that of the 9,300 skilled workers in the study group, only 27 per cent were born in Canada. Does the minister agree with the report's conclusion? It reads in part:
-there is a shortage of upper skilled workers now and it will get more serious as the economy picks up. It does not understate the situation to say that industrial growth in Canada will be inhibited by a lack of skilled workers.
If he agrees with that, can the minister tell the House what specific action he is proposing to take, as the federal Minister of Employment and Immigration, to deal with this situation?

subsubtopic: CRITICISM OF GOVERNMENT TRAINING PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have indicated that substantial additional funding has been made available under apprenticeship programs. Also, I indicated the agreement we have entered into with each of the provinces to see if we can upgrade skills. I have made public the fact that 75 per cent of the highly skilled jobs being filled by immigrants in the manufacturing industry in southwestern Ontario is obviously inappropriate. Because of that, we are weighting our funding and our money into industrial on the job training programs. 1 think that is an appropriate approach.
However, companies have told us that they spend thousands of dollars in training individuals, only to find that when the training is completed they shop around. They would much prefer to do their recruiting from abroad. We have indicated that we will discourage this. If there are Canadians available-and there are jobs available now and there will be in the future-there will be first-class jobs in the particular skills which will be needed by Canada and I should like to see Canadians fill those posts rather than its being done by immigration. I have brought that point home very clearly to my provincial colleagues-all of whom share my concern, I might say.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the same minister. Statistics Canada have indicated that the real level of unemployment is approximately 225,000 persons higher than the government acknowledges, principally because of the inclusion of the category of "discouraged workers". This has a regional impact of profound proportions, because workers in Atlantic Canada and Quebec are more likely to be discouraged with the higher level of seasonal employment there.
Will the minister explain why he said just a moment ago that the current method of measuring unemployment by the labour force survey which excludes these workers is a more accurate indication of the level of unemployment in Canada? Can he explain why he made that assertion?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: STATISTICS CANADA FIGURES-INCLUSION OF "DISCOURAGED WORKERS" CATEGORY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as was indicated, the interpretation, or the misinterpretation of these figures is being done also by the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party. Statistics Canada indicated that the tests were very imperfect and that there was a subjective test made by an individual. Often it is a matter of the question, "Do you want work?" If one goes into a pool room where there are eight guys standing around who are not working, and asks if they want work, they say yes, they want work. Do they want work, or do they want jobs? Statistics Canada indicated that there is a weakness in this basic method of interpreting.
We have indicated the number of discouraged workers according to the labour force survey statistics. These figures have been made available on a monthly basis. We have had the hon. member misinform and "broad-bent" the statistics long enough. I think he is once again doing a disservice in this respect.

subsubtopic: STATISTICS CANADA FIGURES-INCLUSION OF "DISCOURAGED WORKERS" CATEGORY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is complete and utter rubbish. The minister knows that Statistics Canada has made a complete mockery of what he has been telling the people of Canada for the past year. Statistics Canada has just confirmed what I have been saying for a year and a half, that the real level of unemployment is much higher, and now the minister is trying to say Statistics Canada is backing down on its own report. That is absurd.
Considering that Statistics Canada, in the long report I have here-I hope the minister has read it-points out that the figures are, in fact, higher because of seasonal employment patterns in Atlantic Canada and in Quebec, will the minister not agree that Statistics Canada is right, acknowledge he has been wrong, and do something to remedy the situation?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council: it has to do with invitations extended to members to the Royal Family to visit Canada which require the acceptance and approval of the cabinet.
In the last few days, since the Prime Minister left for warmer climes, has the cabinet decided on the request of the government of Ontario to have the Queen Mother attend the Queen's Plate and Dominion Day celebrations?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate receiving the right hon. gentleman's question today because it gives me an opportunity to correct a report which was issued on the weekend, that in some way the government was preventing the Queen Mother from visiting Ontario.
As the right hon. gentleman knows, a number of invitations come in for members of the Royal Family to visit Canada and these have to be considered in respect of the over-all availability of the personage invited. In this particular case, the Queen Mother is being invited to attend the Queen's Plate and possibly some other events in Ontario.
I am sure the right hon. gentleman will recall that last year the same invitation was transmitted, on behalf of the Government of Canada, to the Queen Mother and that, unfortunately, she was unable to come to Canada at the time. At the same time, 1 would like to advise the House that Nova Scotia also has a request in for the Queen Mother to visit that province in association with the international gathering of the clans.
These invitations have been under consideration, and were probably discussed with the Queen Mother by the Prime Minister on the occasion of his visit to London last week. Upon the Prime Minister's return, it should be possible to have answers as to what the program will be.

Oral Questions FORESTRY

Mr. Speaker, I would like to address my question to the Minister of State (Environment). In light of the uncertainty he has created with regard to the future of the forestry service as a result of recent policy changes, changes which are resulting in a mass exodus of scientists and diligent public servants to other industries and other parts of the world, has the minister received iron-clad assurances from the private sector that his privatization scheme is, in fact, working? If not, is he prepared to defer previous decisions to close down the forests products labs and some of the research stations for the reason of lack of money?

Mr. Speaker, I will be making an appropriate announcement very soon. I want to assure the hon. member that our plans for privatization are going fairly well. I also want to tell him that he should be more careful in his choice of words, because not one of the research labs is being closed down. We have six research labs across the country. In terms of the privatization of those two forest products labs, the hon. member should not use the words "closing down". As a result of the planning now going on, and looking at privatization, we hope that once we have completed all the negotiations, those two labs will remain intact and, indeed, their position will be enhanced as a result of working with provincial governments, the private sector and the universities. Their service to the forest industry will, therefore, be enhanced.

I am encouraged by the minister's remarks. I interpret him to mean that the research labs will not be closed down even if his privatization plan does not proceed. I interpret his remarks to mean that his decision to phase out-the federal government's decision-by April 1 is being deferred. Can the minister communicate that comfort to the people who are leaving the department as a result of his decision? Can he, also, make reference to the institutions that are being closed in Ottawa, the Forest Management Institute and the Forest Fire Institute?

Mr. Speaker, there is no change in moving the Forest Management Research Institute to Petawawa: That is going ahead. The Forest Fire Research Institute's move to Petawawa is going ahead.
I have said on previous occasions in this House that we feel, as a result of the amalgamation of the Forest Fire Research Institute and the Forest Management Research Institute in Petawawa, that that facility will become one of the foremost research institutions for forestry in the country. I should also tell the hon. member that we think very highly of the Canadian Forestry Service. It has done an excellent job. I ask the hon. member to just wait for a little while until he hears the announcements we will be making.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. On Friday last the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) entered into discussion of a matter of privilege of which he had given the Chair notice. It related to a regulation made pursuant to sections 4 and 146 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 and its relationship to clause 2 of Bill C-14, an act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act of 1971 which is presently before the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration, or was, at least, at the time the matter was raised.
I listened with great care to the arguments made by the hon. member for St. John's East as he evidently had a serious grievance of substantial significance. I listened as well to the counter arguments put forward by the minister and to supporting arguments put forward on both sides. On Friday, as the
Privilege-Mr. McGrath
House knows, I listened at great length to all members who wanted to participate in the discussion, although 1 did indicate early on that I doubted there were many more significant areas which could be covered.
I was aware, though, that a great many members had different aspects of the question with which they wanted to deal. I refer particularly to the fact that this combination of circumstances, in which, as it was alleged, the bill which is on the order paper contains in one of its clauses what appears to be an intent identical in scope and authority with that of the regulation enacted pursuant to the existing legislation, recently publicized and, more recently, gazetted, has placed a number of people in a somewhat extraordinary situation, as the hon. member pointed out. First, it put a number of hon. members in an awkward situation before the committee and it placed the public in a similarly awkward position in several instances.
That is why I listened to all hon. members who wanted to participate, and with special care to those members who were serving actively on the standing committee. Each of them drew attention to some of the difficulties which had been caused. Since, as I say, I sensed that a substantial grievance may have occurred, I felt obliged to examine the record to determine whether there were procedural steps which could be taken with respect to the grievance, to the difficulty faced by the members and, in turn, by the public, by witnesses before the committee and, particularly, by delegations appearing before it.
Such delegations come to Ottawa with the intention of doing what all of us want us to encourage the public to do, that is, to participate as fully as possible in the democratic process by taking advantage of various stages of legislation or other occasions to come before standing committees of the House to make their views known. To such groups, to hon. members, to delegations, to other witnesses who came and to the general public, both the minister himself and his officials have, I understand, extended regrets and apologies because the combination of the paragraph in the bill and the regulation did place them in an awkward situation.
It is not for me to decide whether or not this apology, expressed both in the House and outside, is sufficient or whether these complications are more severe than that. I do note, however, that an apology was expressed and the minister was, I thought, generous and direct in admitting the difficulty in which he had placed these people. Some members expressed the view that in the circumstances the apology was not sufficient and that other remedies should be sought, one of them being the pursuit of a question of privilege.
Nevertheless, as 1 indicated earlier, it seems to me we are concerned here with matters of law. Did the regulation derive legal authority from the existing act? That is not a question for me to answer. All I know, examining the matter from the point of view of procedure, is that the clause in the bill and the regulation which was published are both in order in terms of the authority of the Chair with regard to procedure. I cannot go beyond this authority and I cannot make a judgment on the legality of the regulation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Warren Allmand (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill S-5, to amend the Canada Business Corporations Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to introduce for second reading Bill S-5, which is legislation to amend the Canada Business Corporations Act. As hon. members know, it is by means of this law that we establish business corporations with limited liability and generally regulate several of their activities. Given that the effective life of the existing act is only three years, this appears at first glance to be an extremely complicated bill. That is, however, misleading. The bill is bulky because it proposes a completely new French version which is being introduced in accordance with an undertaking the government gave to the Quebec Bar in 1975. Most of the
December 11, 1978

other proposed amendments are mere technical changes designed to reconcile conflicts between sections or to fill logical gaps in the system.
On introducing the original bill for second reading in late 1974 the then minister of consumer and corporate affairs characterized the proposed law as comprehensive, clear, equitable, imaginative and, above all, practical. Moreover, during the passage of the bill through parliament departmental officials forecast that the proposed law would not result in any substantial number of new corporations at the federal level and that, in any event, because of the streamlined procedures set out in the bill, the new law could be administered without any substantial increase of resources. Three years of experience have clearly vindicated the minister's high expectations for the act.
The implementation of the new law has proceeded with few administrative complications, and the statute has been well received by the public, businessmen, and their professional advisers across Canada. Indeed, the law has been so well accepted that the forecasts of the officials did not prove to be quite accurate. The number of federal incorporations incorporated each year has increased from 1,800 in 1971 to 5,000 in 1976, the first year of operation of the CBCA, to nearly 8,000 in 1977, and to a projected 10,000 in 1978. In short, the annual federal incorporation activity has increased five-fold since the Canada Business Corporations Act became effective on December 15, 1975.
The officials' optimistic forecast of the administrative efficiencies that would be engendered by the new act proved, however, to be far more accurate. Partly because of the streamlined procedures made possible by the new act and regulations, and partly because of the computerized name search system developed in the department, the corporations branch has been able to handle approximately five times its previous workload with shorter delays and with no substantial increase in resources.
The wide acceptance of the act has not been limited to businessmen and their professional advisers. Provincial corporation law administrators also have been impressed both by its substantive provisions and its procedural mechanisms, and some have accordingly recommended corresponding changes to the provincial law to their respective ministers.
The provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan have already enacted new business corporation laws based on the Canada Business Corporations Act, and at least three other provinces are currently reviewing their acts with a view to adopting many, if not most, of the provisions of the federal law.
It appears, therefore, that the Canada Business Corporations Act is achieving the objectives set for it in section 3, that is, to modernize the federal corporation law and to furnish a model statute that will lead to greater uniformity of corporation law across Canada. To this end, officials of the department did discuss the proposed amendments with several of their provincial counterparts as well as with experts in the
Canada Business Corporations Act private sector to ensure that this increasing tendency towards uniformity is not undermined.
The specific purposes of the proposed amendments are to fulfil two undertakings given by the government during the passage of the act through parliament.

The Department of Justice as well as the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs have undertaken before the Quebec Bar to draft a new French version of the legislation which is not merely a translation of the English text but as much as possible a statement on the legislation in French using the language and ideas with which the members of the Quebec Bar are familiar. The Legislation section of the Department of Justice began in 1975 to redraft the French text of the legislation with the assistance of various legal experts and accountants to prepare the bill now under consideration. On behalf of the government, I would like to thank more particularly the members of the special committee of the Quebec Bar and the lawyers of the Legislation section of the Department of Justice who worked diligently in a rather short period to prepare that new French version.

The second undertaking was given by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to the House Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. That committee was concerned, because of the sweeping substantive changes being effected by the bill, that it might engender many problems for businessmen, lawyers and auditors. The committee, as a condition of approving the bill, therefore insisted that the department return to parliament within a reasonably short time to give the committee an opportunity to review any complaints that have arisen, to consider any proposed amendments to make the act work more equitably and more efficiently and, in particular, to review the broad regulation-making powers granted under section 187 in respect of stock exchange takeover bids.
Fortunately, only one major substantive problem has arisen since the act was implemented; that is, fundamental change, by way of arrangement.
The controversial policy issue, stock exchange takeover bids, has not yet been definitely resolved. Therefore, the government recommends that this issue continue to be dealt with by regulation to ensure maintenance of maximum uniformity among the provisions of the federal corporation law, the provincial securities laws and the stock exchange bylaws that relate to takeover bids through the facilities of a stock exchange or the over the counter market.
Knowing that each substantive provision of the bill will be scrutinized carefully in committee, 1 shall avoid discussing here the relatively minor changes, which may be characterized more as fine tuning than any fundamental change of policy.
The one major substantive change is the introduction in part XIV of the "arrangement" concept. The minister of the day and his officials had consciously omitted this particular tech-

December 11, 1978
Canada Business Corporations Act
nique of fundamental change for two reasons. First, they reasoned that the arrangement institution was superfluous in the act because a corporation could effect any fundamental change by exploiting any one or any combination of the specific fundamental change sections-amendment, amalgamation, continuance, dissolution-set out in the act. Second, they were concerned that the arrangement technique might be exploited to evade the shareholders' right to dissent and so subvert the policy fundation of part XIV.
I must report, however, that experience has proved that an arrangement provision, while perhaps not essential in theory, is a most useful technique to avoid extraordinary formal complications, particularly in respect of the unwinding of an unsuccessful amalgamation or effecting interjurisdictional transfers of corporations.
The government has therefore decided that an arrangement provision should be set out in the act, subject to safeguards that will preclude its use as a technique to squeeze out or freeze out minority shareholders.
The proposed section 185.1 seeks to achieve this goal. Characteristically, the provision gives very broad powers to a court to approve any proposed arrangement. But to ensure maximum protection of minority shareholders, it sets up a high entry threshhold, requiring a proponent of an arrangement to satisfy the court that it is not practicable to achieve the arrangement by use of the more conventional fundamental change institutions.
Moreover, this provision empowers the courts, in any event, to approve a proposed arrangement subject to the condition that any shareholders may dissent from the proposed arrangement and demand payment of the fair value of their shares, a limitation that will clearly discourage improper use of this changed technique in questionable cases.
In sum, although the arrangement provision entails some risks, consonant with the over-all development of the act, the government recommends that it be included in the statute to fulfil a demonstrated need, at least until actual experience proves that such a flexible institution does lead to abuse.
The predecessor bill was originally introduced in the Senate on November 8, 1977, and referred shortly thereafter to the Senate Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce. The committee held several meetings between November, 1977, and February, 1978, to consider the bill, during which time the committee heard the testimony of witnesses from the Department of Justice and the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. The committee concurrently considered some informal briefs that were submitted to the committee chairman while the hearings were in progress. That version was introduced in the House on March 21, 1978, but died on the order paper at the end of the last session.
The present version, Bill S-5, was introduced in the Senate on October 17, 1978, considered by the Senate committee on November 8, and passed by the Senate on November 28. The bill contains 85 substantive clauses, each of which effects an

amendment to a provision of the Canada Business Corporations Act. In light of the testimony presented before the Senate committee, approximately 220 further amendments were made to the bill. About 170 of these amendments were mere language changes to the new French version recommended by a special committee of the Quebec Bar. Most of the remaining 50 amendments were made in response to suggestions of the Senate committee. However, several reflect new suggestions made to the committee or the department during the course of the hearings and during the intervening summer. I should like to thank the Senate committee and its chairman for the diligent and thorough work it has done to improve this bill.
In conclusion, I should point out that the act has been a notable success, that the amendments are largely non-controversial, and that implementation of the proposed new French version at the earliest possible date is highly desirable.
Although I do not want to press hon. members of the House so that they do not have adequate time to consider the bill, 1 should like to underline that the amendments are very technical and that the corporations affected by the act, as well as their technical advisers, are most anxious to see the amendments made. In particular, the proposed amendments to section 26 are required to enable federal corporations to react to amendments to the Income Tax Act effective in late 1977 and imposing December 31, 1978 as a deadline on certain transactions affecting special surplus accounts. Therefore, I recommend that all members of the House support the bill and send it to committee where it can receive detailed consideration as soon as possible.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 will not speak too long on this bill. As the minister said, it is very technical and it is best dealt with at committee. As far as my party is concerned, there is no need to detain the bill very long in the House.
Aside from the amendments made after the bill received consideration in the Senate, the job done on the French version of it was an excellent one. The people in the Department of Justice, the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and the Quebec Bar Association should be commended for the manner in which they have taken this bill and written it so that it can be used effectively in the province of Quebec. We should commend those involved in the handling of the bill.
Other than the French version, the provisions and amendments to the bill are very technical. I do not think I can say much more at this time. When the bill goes before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, I suspect there will be representations made by those concerned with some of the technical amendments. As far as my party is concerned, this bill should pass and be dealt with further at committee stage.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in introducing this bill, the minister pointed out that many of the amendments are of a technical nature. He could have mentioned something about the structure of the bill.
December 11, 1978

On the face of it, the bill amuses me. The government is very interested in the bilingual proposition, yet the entire bill seems to have been rewritten. The English version was written on 42 pages including the French section. Then it switches over and there are 160 pages of only French. Perhaps all the Senators are bilingual and understand what the French section applies to, but suddenly at page 42 the English section stops and all we receive is 160 pages of French with no translation. Perhaps the problem is more severe in the province of Quebec, but the minister opened up the entire bill. All the clauses of the bill have been opened, up and therefore there can be a general discussion. I should like to point out that we should have a general discussion.
This bill was put together from the old corporations act which had been amended by other pieces of legislation. This was brought together under the new Canada Business Corporations Act and put into its present form. There were very few changes and modernizations in the bill. Most of the changes were worth while. They affected the shareholders and their operations within the corporation, as well as relationships among the shareholders, the directors and the corporation. A number of the changes made were for the protection of shareholders. These changes have worked out very well for the shareholders. At the present time they have the right, if necessary, to put their stock on the market at a fair market value, and they can get out of the transaction if they do not agree with the board of directors. At committee stage I would be interested in hearing from the minister how many applications were made for the protection of the act in this sense.
One of the major categories affected by the Canada Business Corporations Act is the people of the country, the consumers and clientele. Very little if anything has been done for these people in Canada. On the other hand, citizens of the United States have been able to go after the large corporations. They have been able to bring before the courts some of the transactions which have taken place in boards of directors meetings, shareholders meetings and in the preparation of data and other paraphernalia which goes into the making of reports to directors and shareholders. They have been able to ascertain, on behalf of the customers of the country, whether a certain corporation was working in a reasonable manner. These facts were not foreign when the act was changed; they were fairly well known by some of the provinces. Therefore, a provision was introduced to appoint an inspector who would look at some of the transactions made by corporations in terms of the directors and shareholders to see whether corporations were working as good citizens or living up to their moral liabilities. Yet this has not happened.
This is no longer 1975 when the act was changed. It is now 1978 and we are approaching 1979. In the last four years a number of things have happened. As a private member, the Minister of State (Multiculturalism) (Mr. Cafik) was interested in some of the machinations of corporations. He became involved in a very meaningful manner. He was concerned about corporations which were manufacturing unsafe products for consumer use. One of the products he was particularly
Canada Business Corporations Act interested in was aluminum wiring. It is interesting to note that in the United States there is a protection in that there is a provision to investigate companies which are producing something that may involve a safety hazard or a customer hazard, or doing something that amounts to a plain dishonest practice, something that corporations sometimes do.
It was suggested by some of my colleagues when this bill was before us in 1975 that we should have an ombudsman who would be able to look at some of the things corporations are doing, things that go beyond shareholder or board of director responsibility. The ombudsman would be appointed by the government with his expenses paid by the corporation he was investigating. This would mean that in Canada we would not have to wait until the United States, as in the case of Firestone tires, said a thing was dangerous and likely to kill people, that it must be recalled and taken off the market. The ombudsman would be able to look at complaints about a company or corporation so that we would have some corporate protection. In this way there could be an investigation and a report to parliament that changes should be made or products should be withdrawn.
This procedure could be followed under an extension of this act or under other acts. The corporate law in the United States is considerably more flexible than ours. The demand in their legislatures is for less secrecy and more openness. Their legislation requires that it is up to the company or corporation to prove that the release of certain information would be against the interest of the state or the interest of the public. Even then, if the government says that because of security reasons it is not in the interest of the state to release certain information, individuals can go to the courts under two or three procedures and obtain the information.
Recently in the United States individuals were able to obtain information about the hazardous aspects of two automobiles. We could not obtain such information in this country, probably for two reasons. First of all, if the government does not know what to do about a certain product or information it stamps it top secret and puts the material in a file. If that does not happen it is probably because the government does not have the information in the first place.
Specifically I am referring to the problem in the United States and in Canada in terms of the Bobcat and Pinto automobiles. It was established in the United States that members of the board of those corporations in their board rooms considered how much it would cost to modify the gas tanks in Bobcats and Pintos. In their wisdom they decided that a lost life was only worth about $475,000, and that would probably be the average for which they were sued. They decided they would probably have to pay for the loss of about 20 lives at that rate, which would amount to about half what it would cost to make the change. This decision was made in the board room by the directors and management.
Under the terms of this act as expanded, the shareholders and customers could probably have found out about that

December 11, 1978
Canada Business Corporations Act
decision. Under this act citizens probably would have the right to inquire about and obtain the background information for that decision.
In the United States citizens are able to obtain that kind of information through court and other procedures, and this has made high court settlements very possible. In one case I believe the amount of $120 million was awarded in respect of death as a result of an accident involving a Pinto. That award has been appealed. Had such a thing occurred in Canada it probably would have required this government to change the act, adding a protection for the general public. I know this government will not do that as it is not the least bit interested in making any kind of survey or inspection results available to the public.
It is of interest to note that people in this country are still driving around with the same kind of tires on their cars as those that were recalled in the United States. People in this country are still driving Genera! Motors and Ford products without dozens of modifications being made, modifications that have been carried out in the United States. I am sure the same is true in respect of washing machines, lawn mowers and almost any product you can name.
There is one particular field that we worry about, and that is in respect of children's toys. We worry about the fact that a toy fashioned after the craft that Lome Green flies around the galaxy shoots a rubber pellet that could cause injury to a child. We worry about that fact, and we worry about whether a child might put his head through the chicken wire on the side of a crib. We have done a very good job in this area, but how anyone is going to get his head through a two-inch wire mesh, I do not know.
It seems all right if adults are involved and are killed on our highways, it seems to be all right if an adult blows himself up as a result of a gas inspection not being carried out, and it seems all right if a house burns down because of faulty wiring, so long as adults are involved. One member of parliament mentioned today that the entire side of an apartment building is sliding into a ravine in Hamilton. He referred also to another case of a building that is only two or three years old and is sinking so fast they almost have to add an additional floor on top. This reminds me of the C. D. Howe method of building the DEW line. When a structure sinks into the permafrost you just add more on top and keep going.
Now that we have had the opportunity of seeing that this act works very well in respect of shareholders and directors, with very few having to pay the big penalties, and that it has brought some stability to the situation, it is time we as reasonable people looked at two other aspects. We should make some changes to provide a protection for the average citizen against a corporation which may be manufacturing shoddy goods. At the present time people have no protection through an inspection procedure, or through access to information about a particular product failure.
There are abuses taking place every day on the part of corporations in other fields. When a small company decides to do something that may be useful in a specific industrial field-

and I am particularly interested in mining-which may put that company into a competitive position with a large corporation, the large corporation immediately takes over that company and the improvement is left dormant. Many of these small companies are swallowed up by the large companies and things that might benefit the consumers are forever lost.
Consumers and consumer benefits are not taken into consideration by those who effect amalgamations. If any consideration is given at all in respect of consumers it is usually detrimental. Citizens should have some protection against such takeovers, amalgamations and the gobbling up of little companies by big ones. They should have protection against this kind of corporate manoeuvre, whatever corporate terminology is used today or even tomorrow. There should be some protection for the individual, the community and the country as a whole. I know this might interfere with the functions of FIRA, but that entity will be noted in history for the four takeovers it stopped and for paying no attention to the hundreds of others that were effected. It does not take very much to convince FIRA what is for the good of Canada.
I suggest that we eliminate FIRA and put its responsibilities under the control of an inspector according to this act. He would probably do a better job as an individual than the whole board of FIRA. It would not surprise me if the Petawawa army base was allowed to be taken over by the United States or China one day simply because FIRA could see some advantages to such a takeover.
I know that all these changes will not be made. This is a lame duck government and we do not expect very much from them anyway. I doubt that they really want to stir up the barrel again.
This bill should have been passed some time ago, but the government could not make up its mind who they would be hurting, who their friends were. I suppose the new changes in the elections act made them totally unsure, but it does not matter one way or the other. We now have an opportunity to look at the corporations bill again and there should be a number of changes made to it.
Something should be done to protect the consumer against the corporate rip-offs which many of these small and large corporations engage in. We should also put in an inspector to determine whether or not the changes being allowed a corporation are advantageous, whether it be a takeover, a roll over, a purchase and so on. Is it a good thing for Power Corporation to take over Argus, or would it be better for Argus to take over Power Corporation? I do not know, but it will make a great difference to many people in this country. Another takeover bid which should be looked into is Simpsons and Sears versus the Bay. Is it to our advantage? Will it increase or reduce the price of shirts?

I was very pleased, Mr. Speaker, to hear the intervention by the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria (Mr. Corbin), and I would like to address my remarks to the same topic. The hon. member was absolutely correct in his comments with respect to the difficulties which have arisen in this country with regard to both languages and the understanding of the laws and rules which apply.
It is extremely appropriate that we in this parliament should do things the way in which we do them in terms of publications by ministers, by committees, etc. I am sure that the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria will agree with me that even though a member of the House may be more familiar with one language than another, it is appropriate for those who are familiar with both to make the comparisons which must be made between the texts of the two languages from time to time. It has been a convenience to the House to be able to look for discrepancies between the two official languages when the English version and French version are side by side. I think there is a great advantage in the publication of the two texts side by side for the purposes of understanding.
It is interesting that this matter should be raised on this particular bill. When I have young people come to visit from my constituency and ask questions about the translation facilities in the House of Commons, I can tell them that this is one of the relatively few places in the country where I can speak in the language in which I am most comfortable and my friend from Madawaska can speak in the language in which he is most comfortable and we can listen to each other and understand each other as we are speaking. It is quite an advantage when one thinks about it. This instantaneous translation facility is an extension of the written translation facility that we have. I understand that was the way in which the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) was speaking. It is interesting in a country like ours to be able to sit in a chamber like this one and no matter in which official language a person speaks he can be understood by every one even though from time to time we do not agree with what we hear. It is an interesting phenomenon nonetheless.
There is another aspect which the hon. member for Timiskaming mentioned that is correct. He stated that when this bill goes to committee it is inevitable that that committee will look at the appendix of the bill and deal with the French version of

Canada Business Corporations Act
the law respecting business corporations, but also I think the committee is likely to take advantage of reviewing the whole of the law with respect to those corporations.
I hope that when the committee does so it will address one of the great problems facing Canadian business today. Whether we like it or not, there is no policy in this country with respect to business and says to Canadian businessmen when dealing with their own government that they will be given a greater opportunity than businessmen from other countries. If that kind of law is reasonable for other countries and is one which we support, greater consideration should be given to supporting it here. This kind of thing has been brought to my attention by businessmen in the electronics field. When dealing with the Department of Supply and Services they have found that the rules are drawn in such a way that struggling businessmen do not have that opportunity, that is, to deal with some advantage with the government of their own country.
I hope the committee will consider this bill in a way that might give that sense of advantage. I do not think it has to be advantage to the point where competition from other countries is excluded. Small businessmen are not asking for that. But they are asking, recognizing differences in our conditions, for equalizers from the point of view of dealing with government. We should look at any bill dealing with the operation of business from that point of view. When we are considering this bill in the committee I hope that we will bear in mind the problems that have affected us because this country has a branch plant economy.
Recently a conference was held in the Conference Centre in Ottawa. This centre used to serve as a railroad station. The conference had as its participants scientists and great thinkers. They talked about the conserver society, but they also talked about the difficulties of research and development. They talked about the difficulty of promoting research and development in a country whose economy has been dominated in other areas by other countries. It is not unusual that that has happened. We are all to blame because we have allowed it to happen. While this government gives lip service to research and to the necessity of developing Canadian business, what does it do to the forest research industry of this country? It cuts it across the throat. That is what it has done. It is in danger not only of harming research in that very important field; it is in danger of setting it back. It will set back experiments and cause Canada to lose its scientists to other countries. The government is discouraging scientific endeavour in Canada. Those are some areas I hope that will be borne in mind when we look at this bill in committee.
We had a budget that affected the business corporations to be governed by this statute to a great degree. Small business has been damaged by the position taken by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). It has been stated that the government will not even consider, at least at this point, rebates with respect to the manufacturer's sales tax.
We have raised in this House of Commons the damage caused to every large sales outlet and business, some of them

governed by this statute, as a result of this government refusing to consider the rebate section. I have automobile dealers in my constituency who say that this measure will cost them $25,000, and it has already affected their current sales. There are appliance sales people in my riding who are affected. Why should these people be made to carry the burden for the government's change of mind? I hope that this matter will be considered, not only with respect to the income tax legislation, but whenever the problems of Canadian businessmen are discussed in the House of Commons.
Then, for some reason or other, the government has decided to close a loophole with respect to a tax advantage given to small corporations. In their discussion they have zeroed in on lawyers, accountants and dentists. The government has not realized that this change will affect artists, artisans, insurance people, in fact a whole range of people who have been advised at great expense to themselves to incorporate. We will consider this in detail when the income tax bill comes forward, but I wonder why a certain segment of business that perhaps deals in unusual ways has been distinguished in some way and set aside. I wonder what kind of consultation this government had with those sectors of the economy it was going to affect. If it had no consultation at all, then they have some time for redemption and the provisions which are set forth in the budget which might affect a segment of Canadian small business might be reconsidered. 1 hope that will happen and I hope Canadian small businessmen affected by that change will get in touch with this government. I hope the government will be flooded with telephone calls, letters and telegrams.
When something like this happened before when dealing with life insurance problems a budget or two ago, the government finally relented. I entreat the government to consider relenting their position on the manufacturers' sales tax and with respect to corporations. It has had a great influence on the business community. I think there is not a person in this House who does not think it important to promote the interest of the working man and woman of this country so that there is a strong, big private business sector, and an equally strong small business sector. Therefore, we should look at what kind of administrative burden this statute puts on the business sector. It is important that we consider it in that way.
Finally, we must consider the question of openness, the above board, cards on the table approach, that the hon. member for Timiskaming spoke of in terms of the business of a corporation. If this does not happen, there is a tendency toward monopoly. Monopolies are not always unhealthy. However, there are some that are.
From time to time in this country we hear that government monopolies are unhealthy, that the intervention of government in business in a monopolistic way is unhealthy. The tendency of corporations that come to the government for licences to become corporations and, therefore, become private, especially when they become large, have a tendency to promote that
December 11, 1978

aspect of monopoly which is not necessarily healthy. I hope we will also consider the bill from that point of view.

The first clause of this bill reads:

The hon. member for Timiskaming has been a tremendous supporter throughout his history in parliament of the use of the French language in this country, of bilingualism and the Official Language Act. 1 do not want to see his position taken out of context and twisted by the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria. He wanted to see both versions, i suppose in order to promote a greater sense of bilingualism, certainly with regard to this bill. I felt those remarks had to be made.
While I am on my feet, there are a couple of other comments I would like to make. When we discussed this legislation before, we were concerned that the legislation did not offer adequate protection to consumers and to customers of corporations in this country. The hon. member for Timiskaming gave a few examples of that. When this bill goes to committee, we should try to build in more protection for consumers in Canada, those who are purchasing goods from corporations.
Large companies in this country have immense power which is becoming greater with the passage of time. A lot of concern is being voiced in Canada, especially by members of the Conservative party, about the growth of government and Crown corporations. Because of that voice from our political right, a lot of attention has been drawn to the role of government in our society. One thing being overlooked is the role of the private sector, which is absolutely immense. When we look at the corporations in Canada, we see that a few very large corporations, particularly in the resource sector, dominate this country. A lot of these are foreign-owned multinationals which are extremely powerful. 1 need only look at a few examples close to me, such as the grain business. It is dominated by five very large companies. The Wheat Board, the grain pools and these very large grain companies hold the power.
Canada Business Corporations Act
We can also look at the way some of the food companies dominate the food business in this country. We see the tremendous impact they have on the life of the ordinary consumer. I could give many examples of that. The minister, being a progressive left wing or pink Liberal-I do not know which is the best adjective-is frustrated by the lack of power he has in the law with regard to fighting the power of some of these large corporations. He has said on occasion that he would like more power with regard to protecting the consumers of this country against some of the tremendous powers of the very large corporation.
At the present time we have a commitment from the minister to call in the heads of food companies to explain why their profits are so great. I know he is concerned about a number of things such as the rise in bread and turkey prices. When we discuss a bill like this in committee, we have to look at the power of these corporations. We must do this collectively so far as very large companies are concerned.
Another point that should be made may have been made by the hon. member for Timiskaming, I am not quite sure. Since this bill passed the other place, we have learned that several large automobile companies have secret warranties covering such items as rust, the deterioration of engine parts and the like. This matter came to my attention just recently when I was concerned about the phasing out of premium or super unleaded gasoline. When we examine this bill we should be concerned about corporate secrecy.
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) recently made quite a name for himself on a good issue, that of government secrecy. The other side of the coin is corporate secrecy. Much of what is conducted by large corporations is secret. When I try to pursue a matter having to do with food or agriculture, I am frustrated by the secrecy of large companies. I have looked at what is happening in the food business and what companies are doing in terms of altering food, refining it and so on. Consumers often ask me what goes into their food. They ask how it is changed, how it is preserved, what additives and what chemicals are included. Most of that is kept secret by I. T. and T. and others involved in big business. When you try to get that information, it is like hitting your head against a brick wall. It is nearly impossible to get any information. I suggest we look at that aspect of companies in terms of corporate secrecy.
Many people say we have no business doing that, that the government is spending taxpayers' money, that it is involved publicly and in that way it is a public cost. I can argue on the other side, that a corporation is also spending taxpayers' money. They are spending consumer dollars. What difference does it make? Even the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling), who spoke on behalf of the Conservative party, has to eat. Therefore, he should be concerned about corporate secrecy as well.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be very short. I would like to refer to the comments of the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria (Mr. Corbin) and only to that. The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) and the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) have already pointed out the importance of clause 1 of Bill S-5. The first paragraph of clause 1 of the bill reads as follows:
1. (1) The French version of the Canada Business Corporations Act is repealed and the version set out in the schedule to this act is substituted therefor.

We have every reason to wonder why this approach should have been taken to producing a French version of an act which figures in the consolidated statutes of 1974, 1975 and 1976, chapter 33. I am not sure whether the minister addressed himself to this aspect during the course of his remarks because, unfortunately, I was out of the chamber doing some research. Whether or not there were some serious errors in the French version, as I suspect, I may say one has noticed such before in translations from one language to another. Frequently we find variations between the text of English and French versions of statutes which would cause a great inconvenience to anyone in a court of law trying to decide which version ought to be followed in a particular case.
The most notable example which occurs to me relates to a bill on the fisheries. Just as a matter of interest, I counted up the number of definitions in the English version and compared

it with the number in the French version. There were 12 definitions in the French text, and only 11 in the English, or it may have been the other way around. This looks to me very much like laxity, a lack of care in the translation process, which needs to be watched very carefully. Unnecessary problems can be created if definitions do not correspond. It is only recently that the definitions have been given following the English alphabet and, in the French version, following the French alphabet. That is fair enough. Definitions are easier to look up that way. Until very recently they followed either one pattern or the other and the translations were opposite one another.
1 find it extraordinary that there should have been such serious errors that the French version had to be withdrawn and replaced with a new one as an annex. The indifference of the translators to this question ought to be underlined. All ministers should take particular care to ensure that when bills are put before the House the French and English versions correspond entirely and there is no chance of misinterpretation on this ground.

Mr. Speaker, I think I should take a few minutes to answer some of the questions hon. members have raised and to correct certain misunderstandings.
The appearance of the complete French version in the schedule is due to a situation which arose after the enactment of the new Canada Business Corporations Act in 1975. That act was first drafted in the English language, as was the common practice up to that time, and then translated into French. When the bill was brought to parliament and examined by French-speaking lawyers, particularly by the Bar of Quebec, it became evident there was a good deal of criticism of the French expressions used in the law. Members of the House finally agreed to let the bill go through in the English and French versions on the understanding that the minister of the day would take the raw material of the act and have it drafted de novo in French. So what we have in the schedule is not simply an altered French version; it is, in terminology and expression, a version acceptable to the French speaking lawyers of this country. We worked closely with the Quebec Bar on this project and the draftsmen were French speaking.
Many statutes are now prepared along those lines; the raw material is drafted in English and French and experts in both languages make sure that the final version has the same meaning. What we have in this instance is a version prepared by draftsmen rather than by translators. I agree with the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) that it is very helpful in committees of the House to be able to refer to the English version side by side with the French version. The English version can be found in the Revised Statutes-there has been no change, basically, there-but we shall try to arrange that both versions are available so that hon. members who wish to do so may follow them side by side.


December 11, 1978

Certain other matters related to corporations were mentioned; for example, securities and taxation questions, mergers, foreign takeovers and so on. I consider these to be very important matters but for the most part they are dealt with under other statutes. In Canada, securities legislation is provincial whereas in the United States it is federal.
The hon. member for Timiskaming referred to securities legislation and to the law in the United States. 1 would remind him that in Canada securities legislation is provincial. Then again, matters relating to the taxation of corporations are dealt with under the Income Tax Act and related measures; for instance, budgetary measures introduced by the Minister of Finance. Mergers are dealt with under the combines legislation. Foreign takeovers are dealt with by FIRA and CALURA deals with corporate reporting. So, while all these things are important, they are not the basic subject matters of the corporations act. The basic subject matters of the corporations act are the incorporation of companies and the rules which relate to shareholders, boards of directors, the publishing of prospectuses and so forth.
I wanted to clear up some of the misunderstanding with respect to the French version in the schedule and also to point out that, while we consider these other matters with respect to incorporations important, they are not usually found in the corporations act. One must remember that corporations, as legal entities, must obey all other laws.
Motion agreed, bill read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
