speakeroldname: Hon. Warren Allmand (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: CANADA NON-PROFIT CORPORATIONS ACT MEASURE RESPECTING CHARITABLE CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
that Bill S-4, respecting Canadian nonprofit corporations, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to introduce for second reading Bill S-4, which would amend our law relating to non-profit corporations. Like Bill S-5, which is legislation to amend the Canada Business Corporations Act, this bill also appears to be a long and complex one, but its size belies its actual content. It is in fact largely a repetition of the Canada Business Corporations Act but modified to make the uniform provisions apply specifically to non-profit corporations and to add a number of new provisions which are essential and which apply uniquely to such corporations.
Of the total of about 1 5,000 non-profit organizations carrying on their activities in Canada about 3,000 are federal non-profit corporations. To give the House and the country some examples of these, I will mention the Canadian National Institute for the Blind, the United Way or Centraide, the Canadian Heart Foundation, the Canadian Medical Associa-
Non-profit Corporations
tion, the Canadian Cancer Society, Hockey Canada and the Vanier Institute. These are but a few examples of our many federal non-profit corporations.
Although small in number, because many of them carry on their activities across Canada and are perceived as Canadian as distinct from local institutions, their impact on Canadian social life is enormous. That is the principal reason why these institutions merit the special attention of parliament.
On being advised by the authors of the Canada Business Corporations Act proposals that they would recommend enactment of a new statute to apply only to business corporations, in 1970 the department retained Professor Peter Cumming of Osgoode Hall Law School and instructed him to prepare a report on a proposed statute to apply uniquely to non-profit corporations. Professor Cumming undertook immediately to analyze the activities of non-profit corporations in Canada as well as the content of several modern, non-profit corporation laws, and in particular those of the State of New York. Professor Cumming submitted his report to the department in 1973. The department published the report in 1974 under the title "Proposals for a new not-for-profit corporations law for Canada". Like the business corporation proposals which preceded it, the report was presented in the form of a model act accompanied by a second volume of section by section commentary.
Immediately after their publication the department distributed copies of the proposals to a large number of federal non-profit corporations, to the managers of non-profit organizations and to a number of lawyers and accountants who participate actively in the administration of the affairs of non-profit organizations, requesting their comments on the proposed model act.
The department received several major briefs and a large number of specific comments on the proposals and, working in close collaboration with the legislative section of the Department of Justice, began in 1975 to draft a statute in accordance generally with the proposals but modified in the light of the critical comments received. The department's plan was to table the bill at once after passage of the Canada Business Corporations Act in late 1975 to bring the non-profit corporation law into line with the new business corporation law. But because of the criticism of the French version of the Canada Business Corporations Act on which the non-profit corporation law is based, the minister had to defer completion of the bill on non-profit corporations until the new French version of the business corporation law was completed.
The proposals contained three main recommendations. The first was that parliament should enact a discrete act to apply to non-profit corporations which parallels in all respects the business corporation law except that provisions must be modified or added to deal with the specific requirements of nonprofit corporations. The second recommendation was that the non-profit corporation law should be characterized with respect to the purposes of the two kinds of non-profit corporations, charitable corporations and membership corporations, and not with respect to the lack of power of such a corporation

December 11, 1978
Non-profit Corporations
to issue shares. The third major recommendation was that the proposed law should apply to all federal non-profit corporations including, as well as those corporations subject to Part II of the Canada Corporations Act, all non-profit, special act corporations and all corporations subject to the Boards of Trade Act.
The bill, therefore, by design parallels very closely most of the substantive and formal provisions of the Canada Business Corporations Act. As a result, it raises very few new policy issues. Generally what the proposed law seeks to accomplish is to modernize the federal non-profit corporation law and to set out substantive rules and procedures which are familiar to all corporate managers, their professional advisers and government administrators.
The proposed law above all seeks to establish a system that gives non-profit corporation managers broad, flexible powers to manage, subject to the rights of the members of such corporations to participate effectively in the management of non-profit corporations' affairs and to check any abuses by directors or officers.
Because of the extremely technical nature of the bill 1 do not propose to discuss any specific provisions of the bill at this time, with the understanding that these can be discussed in committee. I would like, however, to mention several of its principal characteristics.
First, consonant with our general concepts of freedom of association in Canada the bill permits incorporation as of right, subject only to the condition that its express or implied purposes must not contravene any law of Canada, particularly the Canadian Bill of Rights.
Second, the single distinguishing characteristic of a nonprofit corporation is that, except in narrowly specified cases, it cannot pass through any of its money or property to its members. It can carry on business and may earn profits but, if it does so, any such profits must be applied to further its charitable or membership purposes.
Third, the proposed law distinguishes between the two basic types of non-profit corporations. The first is the charitable corporation which carries on activities which are primarily for the benefit of the public. With respect to financial disclosure it is cast under the bill as an analogue of a business corporation which distributes securities to the public. The second is the membership corporation which carries on activities primarily for the benefit of its members. Under the bill, for the purposes of financial disclosure it is cast as an analogue of a closely held business corporation. It must make full financial disclosure to its members but not to the public.
Fourth, the present Canada Corporations Act characterizes a non-profit corporation as a corporation without share capital. Although the proposed law abandons this characterization to focus on the function of a non-profit corporation, it continues to prohibit a non-profit corporation from issuing shares, since ownership of shares connotes a right to dividends and to share in any liquidation distribution of property of a corporation.

Fifth, the bill does expressly empower a non-profit corporation to issue debt obligations and, subject to qualification of any prospectus by a provincial securities commission, to distribute its debt obligations to the public.
Sixth, like the Canada Business Corporations Act, the bill requires extensive financial disclosure in accordance with proposed regulations.
Seventh, it clarifies the rights of an aggrieved member to a fair hearing in any case where the corporation proposes to discipline him or terminate his membership. It also simplifies the procedures that enable an aggrieved member to seek judicial review of any such action by a corporation.
Eighth, and finally, the bill deals with the distribution of any remaining property of a non-profit corporation on liquidation and dissolution. In the case of a charitable corporation a liquidation distribution must be made in accordance with the corporation's articles or, if the articles contain no such provisions, then to another charitable corporation that has similar purposes and that is approved by a court. In the case of a membership corporation, a liquidation distribution must be made in accordance with the articles or, if the articles contain no such provision, then rateably to the members existing at the time of liquidation and dissolution.
Because the two laws are so closely related, the Senate Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce considered together both Bill S-5, the CBCA amendment, and the present bill, Bill S-4. The Senate committee conducted several hearings on the bill, heard witnesses both from the private sector and the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, and recommended a number of amendments in the light of the testimony presented to it.
To maintain the bill parallel with the Canada Business Corporations Act, the Senate committee made some 30 general amendments as well as some 100 amendments to the French version. In addition, in response to the briefs presented to it, the Senate committee made four substantial amendments. The first was to legitimize indirect voting provisions such as those set out in the constitution of the Red Cross. The second was to simplify the holding of members' meetings outside Canada, which renders the policy of the bill consistent with the government's policy of encouraging foreign non-profit organizations to meet in Canada. The third requires a membership corporation that has solicited moneys from the public or obtained a grant from government to make public financial disclosure as does a charitable corporation. Finally, the Senate committee approved an amendment that excepts a board of trade or chamber or commerce from the right to dissent, treating those organizations differently from other membership corporations on the ground that their functions are unique.
The predecessor bill, Bill S-3, was passed by the Senate in March, 1978 and introduced in the House on April 3, 1978. It did not proceed to second reading and hence died on the order paper at the end of the third session.
Although the bill does not revolutionize the federal law relating to non-profit corporations, like the Canada Business
December 11, 1978

Corporations Act it does attempt to clear away a great many conceptual myths, to eliminate unnecessary formalities, and to render compliance with and administration of the law efficient.
In sum, the proposed law attempts to create a system that assures members and public contributors will be treated fairly, that permits members to participate effectively in the administration of a corporation's affairs, and that, equally important, enables corporate managers to achieve the purposes of such corporations effectively. Thus, like the Canada Business Corporations Act, this statute, although quite long, is clear, comprehensive, and practical.
Therefore, I recommend the bill to the House and hope for its quick passage so it can go to committee for detailed examination as soon as possible.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I look forward to seeing the minister's bill go to committee, as the minister indicated, because, although the bill does not raise any specific policy issues, it raises some general policy issues with which I would like to deal. It is also extensive in terms of its attempt to deal with a staggering variety of non-profit corporations and other organizations in what might be called the volunteer area in our society.
I note in particular that, when the matter went to the other place, considerable discussion took place with respect to the role that some of the organizations might play. I think as we go down the road over the next couple of years, we will find that the role of the non-profit corporation will increase, not only in the area of social policy, as the minister has indicated, but indeed in a variety of other ways, as has already been the case.
Part of the difficulty in discussing this subject is that we tend to look on non-profit corporations as being not entirely productive. They are organizations which we need because their activities are not part of the normal economic transactions in our society. That is something with which we will have to cope very soon.
In connection with that subject, a very good essay was written recently for the Vanier Institute of the Family which puts the matter in good capsule form. Most of us accept the fact that the really important things done in society are done in the resource sector, the manufacturing sector or the services sector, but very often we forget that all of that is held together by what some people refer to as the household and community sector. I dislike the word "sector," but it is one that is used here.
Let me quote from this essay what 1 think is a very useful and thoughtful comment. Let us suppose we looked at all the activities which have no value in the marketplace and which do not come under the category of the gross national product, and let us see what it would cost us if we exacted a price for them. I refer to the various things done in the household and in the community. The following is a quote from Hugh Stretton, an Australian political scientist, who said:
Non-profit Corporations
How easily we could turn the tables on the economists if we all decided that from tomorrow morning, the work of the domestic economy should be paid for.
The reference here is to everything that is done in the household and in the community. The quotation continues:
Instead of cooking dinner for her own lot, each housewife would feed her neighbours at regular restaurant rates; then they'd cook for her family and get their money back. We do each other's housework and gardening at award rates. Big money would change hands when we fixed each other's tap washers and electric plugs at the plumbers' and electricians' rates. Without a scrap of extra work the gross national product would go up by a third overnight. We would increase that to half if the children rented each other's backyards and paid each other as play supervisors, and we could double it if we all went to bed next door at regular massage parlour rates.
I might add that that is a quote. I continue:
Our economists would immediately be eager to find out what line of investment was showing such fabulous growth in capital/output ratio. They'd find that housing was bettered only by double beds and they'd recommend a massive switch of investment-
To the household and community sector.
That is very important because for a long time we have not recognized that all the work which passes for real endeavour in the household and in the community does not fit our economic categories. Anybody who has been in this place for any longer than a week understands that the gross national product is the real trinity of this place. Of course, you can increase or deflate the g.n.p. and accomplish nothing in the process. That is why more and more people will find the use of the non-profit corporation to be of real value to the community. Whatever the changes are in relation to the non-profit corporation, they must be helpful to specific groups.
I went through Bill S-4 as quickly as I could because I only received it this morning, but I could not find anything in it specifically related to non-profit housing corporations. I do not know if they are included in the bill, but some portions of them are assumed to be included in the act. There are non-profit corporations in the housing field which relate to municipalities so that some municipalities have their own non-profit housing corporations. Those organizations are entirely different from a series of private non-profit housing corporations. For example, they have different capital, funding sources, modus operandi and mandates from church groups, labour unions and service clubs.
Even though these people want to contribute to society in areas other than their specific mandates, it should be remembered that private non-profit housing corporations are very, very different from public non-profit corporations. There is nothing in the bill dealing with that area. By indirection the government, without perhaps thinking about it, almost annihilated private non-profit housing corporations. The government did not realize this because it was not paying attention to the fact that it was a different kind of operation, with a different corporate structure.
The same is true respecting the field of culture. 1 am sure the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) will make comments in that regard. The bill primarily deals with changes as they affect very large non-profit and volunteer corporations.

December 11, 1978
Non-profit Corporations
The discussion in the other place dealt with the Red Cross, boards of trade and chambers of commerce, very large and traditional organizations. But the bill does not contemplate non-profit organizations which will emerge in the near future because of a variety of concerns and needs.
I should like to refer to the very good study "People in Action", a report of the National Advisory Council on Voluntary Action to the Canadian government of one year ago. Using 1975-76 figures, approximately $200 million was spent by the government, divided into 52 programs in 24 departments. Very often when groups are looking for grants, tax advantage or some non-monetary advice on getting into business to serve particular needs, they hardly know where to turn. Although the changes in the act are good for non-profit corporation lawyers, most people find the act difficult to comprehend.
I should like to turn to clause 109 in the bill which specifically deals with the indirect vote. When the other place dealt with this matter, it was quite properly concerned that an organization such as the Red Cross could not gather together all its members in order to have an election of officers and conduct its business. The Red Cross has approximately 80,000 members. It was estimated that it would cost $300,000 in order to bring all the members together in one place at one time. It was felt that the Red Cross could use that $300,000 more productively towards the needs of Canadians, rather than organizing its business meeting. In large sectors across the country, the Red Cross elects certain delegates. Those delegates elect other delegates, and by the time they get through the pyramid, approximately 75 members do the voting.
The clause which allowed for indirect voting was adopted. It is a very good provision for organizations such as the Red Cross. It makes sense, given the size of that organization and the fact that people know it, trust it and depend upon it. Its members do not have to worry about decisions taken which affect them. However, that clause applies to new non-profit housing corporations.
From my experience in this area, I can assure the House that the members should have more control than the clause provides. For a smaller organization of approximately 50 or 60 people which does not have a position of trust gained over time in a particular community, clause 109(3) allows for an oligarchic situation whereby a small number of people control the organization. If nothing else, the touchstone of a non-profit corporation, particularly one which deals in a voluntary manner, is that it must be accountable to its membership. It is absolutely essential that the membership not be shut out by what can be construed to be appropriate indirect election. When it comes to the crafting of corporate legislation for non-profit organizations, it is essential in the name of uniformity that we do not create more difficulties than we have had in the past, particularly if we get into the situation whereby there are more and more of those corporations.

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act in order to change the current boundaries and include the Eastern Townships.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as we heard it, the motion I am putting forward today reads as follows:
That in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act in order to change the current boundaries and include the Eastern Townships.
The so-called select territory now includes Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and that portion of the province of Quebec that is south of the St. Lawrence River and east of Quebec Highway 23, being the highway connecting from Levis through St-Georges de Beauce with the Maine boundary.
December 11, 1978

Mr. Speaker, the motion gives us an opportunity to remind the government that areas such as the eastern townships can no longer wait that the great economic and industrial strategies bring about the results expected by the government itself. In other words, we can wait no longer and, as responsible government members, it is not good enough to attack current government strategies. We must advocate immediate and fast implementation of regional strategies, with special provisions for the economically and socially needy areas.
The motion put forward proposes one thing only: amending the current boundaries to include the eastern townships, more specifically the area within a 30-mile radius from Sherbrooke and the eastern part of that city, that is the area bordering all of Highway 1 up to the American border. I could hardly understand someone opposing this, because it would be running counter to the purpose of the current act, questioning its validity and efficiency. In other words, what I am asking for is that an area with competent and hard-working industrialists and a local manpower that can and wants to work be allowed to produce the goods it can make. Of course, producing is not enough because the goods must be sold, and they must be sold at competitive prices. But if to the real costs of production the real and significant transportation costs are to be added, given the distances, we must admit that we are ruining our regional economies, that we are literally emptying our regions and in fact it is totally unacceptable. The great economic and industrial strategies of the government are designed for well to do municipalities and we must demand henceforth that strategies be elaborated for vulnerable regions, that is for poor regions which are running the risk of becoming even poorer. I concede that the proposition I am making today is a very weak weapon to fight back the heavy pressures brought to bear upon us by the present state of the economy.
The motion before us today allows me to raise questions which would normally call for answers, yet these answers cannot be dilatory but must rather be responsible, comprehensive and practical. The first, and maybe I should say the only question is the following: is it necessary to raise the issue of an individual's right to work and whether this issue is restricted to a given area of Canada? Of course, one day we can talk about the right to prosperity and the distribution of this prosperity.
However, to raise the issue of everybody's basic entitlement to a job is perhaps like engaging a dialogue of the deaf and, if one happens to sit on the government benches, he is running the risk of being told that he is speaking like a member of the opposition. I think it is time the government considered the right to work is a top priority because it is the main cause of the present anxiety, and particularly in areas where job creation is more a matter of chance than of economic and industrial strategy.
Freight Assistance
It must be acknowledged, however, that if it is up to the government to take the lead as far as the recognition and the organization of the right to work are concerned this right will come out of a consensus, particularly at the level of economic agents. Present strategists, and in particular economists, place a large share of the responsibility on ordinary workers, and they do not hesitate to ask them to tighten their belts and to be reasonable, making them believe that it is the only solution. It is probably part of it but it is high time workers could count on spokesmen who will state to everyone that they are not solely responsible for the economic balance and that they will not be the only ones to accept restraints that one can easily agree with them to find unacceptable.
The workers are willing to understand but to them logic lies primarily in facts. For example, how can we explain the sense of social responsibility of a company such as Cadbury which did not hesitate to lay off 500 people for reasons that are difficult to explain and are most certainly embarrassing both for the company itself and for all those who need social conscience as a law for the operation of democracy. In Canada when we ask the workers to co-operate, we ask them first to tighten their belts, and finally to move or to expatriate themselves. Strategists call this mobility and recycling. I am in favour of mobility and recycling, provided there is a possibility of choice. If it becomes a utopia to long for happiness, we should at least have a say in our misfortunes.
Mr. Speaker, the motion I move today provides an opportunity to remind the government that there are needs throughout Quebec to which nobody brings adequate answers and for which government measures are inadequate, if not inexistent. My suggestion today is thus essentially constructive, and even if it is only a means, nobody can question its effectiveness, provided its application in the long term is guaranteed.
I have already mentioned the creation of a department of rural development, the setting up of a developmental infrastructure, the necessity of regional strategies for economic and industrial expansion. This, Mr. Speaker, is the motivation behind the motion which I have moved today, because I feel it can serve as a basis for the right to work. I must proclaim before this government that Canadians want to work and that we must do our utmost to make it possible for them to work, especially in the eastern townships region. To reach this aim, we need our own financial resources, including the budgets which will allow us to create permanent jobs at a minimal cost.
That is the challenge I am now asking the government to accept, and I suggest that the amendment I am proposing today is tangible evidence that the government is prepared to consider our particular needs, especially when it means the right to work for people who are able and willing to work.

I see the hon. member for Bonaven-ture-lles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bechard) who is also one of his colleagues from Quebec and who I imagime will not hesitate to urge the parliamentary secretary to favour the passage of this measure so it will be examined in committee, and in any case, no one doubts that many members from Quebec and others from both sides of the House will be interested in having an excellent discussion in committee and perhaps open a very valid discussion on other sectors in Quebec and other sectors in Canada. speechtext:
It is a pleasure, Mr. Speaker, for me to rise on this motion:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act in order to change the current boundaries and include the eastern townships.
I can understand the problem of the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Tessier). However, I do think that the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act has been designed primarily and specifically for the Atlantic region, the Gaspe peninsula and the lower south shore of the St. Lawrence River. In these areas transportation is a problem, and that becomes very clear
December 11, 1978

when one leaves Montreal and proceeds along the south shore into the eastern provinces.
I also feel that the hon. member's problem is not only related to transportation but also to the economic and social growth within the eastern townships. The geographical area of the eastern townships is much closer to the markets in Montreal and to the west of Montreal.
This motion affords me the opportunity to review the usefulness of this program. As a member of parliament from the Atlantic region, I have watched closely the effects this program has had on my own province of Nova Scotia and how it fits into the national transportation policy. The Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act is, in my opinion, a very good piece of legislation for the promotion of regional development in the Atlantic region, the Gaspe and the lower south shore of the St. Lawrence River. A fundamental principle of our national transportation policy is enshrined in this act, and that is the principle of equity between the various modes of transportation which support regional development and allow us to establish markets to compete with other areas in Canada.
The essential purpose of this legislation, introduced into the House in 1969 by the then minister of transport who is presently Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson), was to extend to the trucking mode the intra and westbound subsidy programs provided for under the Maritime Freight Rates Act. Until that time, only the commodities shipped by rail benefited from the subsidies. The provincial governments concerned, the trucking industry and members from all parties recognized the need for such legislation, and it has contributed to the further development of a viable and efficient trucking industry in the select territory, which includes Newfoundland, P.E.I., New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and the portion of Quebec which is south of the St. Lawrence River and east of highway 23 for the trucking mode, and Diamond Junction and Levis for the rail mode. In so doing, it allowed for a better utilization of transportation resources.
If one looks at the various subsidies paid out, one is struck by the very rapid increase in subsidy payments for the movement of commodities by truck.
For example, in 1971-72, $7 million was paid to the trucking mode for both intra and westbound commodity movements. In 1977-78 these payments reached $26.5 million. In addition, in 1974 a 20 per cent selective westbound subsidy was added and the payments have grown from $0.7 million in 1974-75 to $1.5 million in 1977-78.
During that same period of time, from 1971 to 1978, subsidies paid for the rail programs under the Maritime Freight Rates Act, both intraregional and westbound, grew at a less rapid pace, from approximately $13 million to $16 million. As in the case for the trucking mode, it should be noted that the selective westbound subsidy also applies to the rail mode and for that particular subsidy, payments have grown from $0.9 million to $1.9 million. The total subsidy payments under the Maritime Freight Rates Act and the
Freight Assistance
Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act amounted to $45.9 million in 1977-78 and it is estimated that the payments will be higher in 1978-79, principally, due to the increased movements of coal, pulp and paper products and other manufactured goods. The increasing amount of subsidy paid is a reflection of rate or tariff increases as well as growth in the volume of shipments originating in the select territory.
In 1970 we saw the establishment of the federal-provincial committee on Atlantic region transportation. Since then there has been a very high level of co-operation between the provinces concerned and the federal government on these matters and, as a matter of fact, on a wide range of transportation initiatives.
The general trend in so far as these subsidy programs are concerned has been to make them more selective and more responsive to economic and industrial development strategies as designed and implemented by the provinces with the support of the federal government. Members will agree that, in a great number of cases, it does not make economic sense to subsidize the shipment of raw material out of the select territory and then, months later, see them return to the region in the form of various finished products. This, of course, is only a general observation and may not apply to all cases, but given the various factors related to determining the location of firms, or trade patterns and that sort of thing it is a very important one.
This is in fact one of the reasons why the federal-provincial committee on Atlantic region transportation was established. Federal and provincial officials guided by their respective governments now look closely at each application for the selective westbound subsidy and make recommendations as to the advisability of including a given commodity under the program based on a number of criteria. Generally speaking, the aim is to select commodities which are highly sensitive to transportation costs, that have or display a potential for maximum value added in the region, and that are related to the development strategies of the provinces concerned.
As members know, until September 1, 1978, the intraregional subsidy program was a blanket program covering virtually all commodities shipped within the select territory, the select territory including Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and that portion of the province of Quebec which I have already outlined.
In 1972 a major study was undertaken by the committee which aimed generally at identifying in some detail the main commodities moving intraregionally by rail and truck. More precisely, the objective of the study was to identify the commodities for which the existing intrasubsidy was playing a significant role, or conversely, where the subsidy contribution was so small as to be insignificant. This information, together within other transportation and economic data, was subsequently used as the basis for the design of a revised intrasubsidy program.
Following ministerial meetings and extensive consultation with the provinces, shippers, the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission, the Atlantic Provinces Trucking Associa-

December 11, 1978
Freight Assistance
tion and the railways, the federal minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) announced in December, 1977, the introduction of major improvements to the intraregional rail and trucking subsidy program to be effective September 1, 1978.
Let me summarize, Mr. Speaker, the essential elements of these changes. The most far-reaching one, I believe, is that the intraprogram no longer provides for a blanket subsidy. The program is now selective in the sense that it only applies to a list of eligible commodities or eligible commodity groups that are produced in the region. It should be noted that although selective, there are still a large number of commodities covered; in fact, most are covered by the program. As in the case of the 20 per cent additional selective westbound subsidy introduced in 1974, most farm products, forest products and fresh fish and other marine products are eligible. This reflects recognition of the importance of these sectors to the economic base of the region. In addition, several other primary products and most manufactured goods are also eligible. This new trend away from the blanket-type subsidy will ensure that subsidy funds are spent more effectively and that transportation assistance will be far more responsive to the needs of the region.
The new intraprogram provides a level of assistance equal to 15 per cent of the rates which would normally apply. Also to help ease the transition to the new program, a phase-out period was introduced for those commodities that are no longer eligible. For them, a provisional level of assistance equal to IV2 per cent is being paid beginning September 1, 1978, and will last until August 31, 1979, thereafter being reduced to zero.
Finally, and this is also an important aspect of the changes brought to this program, the intrasubsidy has been extended to the air and marine modes. In so doing, all carriers are treated more equitably and shippers will benefit from a wider choice of transportation modes.
However, Mr. Speaker, there is one criticism in this area from persons concerned and from the shipping industry in the Atlantic area and that is that an appeal procedure has not yet, been put into effect. It seems that transport officials have promised an appeal procedure, but the effort of getting it in place seems to be slow. This would benefit those people who have had their commodities excluded in the east. They could have them looked at and the shipper could have his case heard on a certain product. Provinces are saying that they cannot help a shipper in the area because the appeal procedure has to be set up at this level.
It is important to underline that the effect of the new subsidy program does not amount to a net loss in payments to the region. In effect, the savings incurred as a result of the new program are being reallocated to other essential priority transportation projects and programs in the region.
It is in that context that the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Program was announced in 1977. Under this program the federal government proposed to spend up to $125 million within a period of three years, to help improve transportation services in the four Atlantic provinces.

This program is designed to upgrade the primary highway network, $32 million to be put into Nova Scotia by the federal government as well as $32 million to be matched by the province. The province, of course, has determined the priorities of which highways. I know that many parts of highways 101 and 103 are being covered under this program.
The program is also to improve transportation and to rationalize freight and passenger subsidy payments within the region. The new intrasubsidy program is in fact part of this package. It may also be worth mentioning that studies are now beginning with regard to the westbound freight subsidy program in order to determine its effectiveness in promoting regional development.
There is some criticism from people in the area who are most concerned, those in industry, that they will not be given the opportunity, before a program is put in place, to be consulted by Transport Canada officials. As we know, this happened with proposed changes that were announced in December, 1977. After eight months of hard work with industry, they were changed to the satisfaction of industry. It is hoped this will not happen again and that the various groups in the Atlantic region and Gaspe Peninsula will be approached this time. As I said, the program includes a major highway strengthening program to which the federal government will contribute $100 million for the costs of approved projects. It also includes a passenger transportation program designed to improve the network of intercity bus service. Of the $25 million total, $4 million is to go to the bus service. However, I understand no proposal has yet been sent by the province of Nova Scotia for improvements to this intercity bus service.
There is also included in this program improvements to local and regional airports, as well as improvements to viable rail passenger services.
The federal government will contribute $25 million over the three years toward bus and airport improvements and, through the national rail passenger policy, a 100 per cent payment of operating deficits on those rail passenger services which are retained as essential.
In summary, since the adoption of the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act in 1969, the federal government, with the full co-operation of the provinces concerned, has introduced several measures to ensure that transport subsidies become an efficient tool, in promoting regional development and also contribute to the rationalization and improvement of the transportation system in our part of Canada. I share the concern of the hon. member for Compton. However, one has to look at the objectives, as I have outlined them, in the proposed legislation to see' how, over a period of years, they have become effective in a given area of transportation because of distance. The motion implies that transportation costs are an important factor for economic and industrial development in the Eastern Townships. Only a detailed survey of all the industries in the region will reveal to what extent their products are sensitive to transportation costs and, to what extent these costs are a determining factor in lowering their ability to compete in various markets.
December 11, 1978

The Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act has taken a long time to get where it is today and to be acceptable to shippers of the area. In the future there will be other areas and problems to be ironed out. Perhaps the hon. member should look for a study to see whether his area comes under the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the motion of the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Tessier). I intend to resume my seat well before six o'clock. I hope the House will agree with the subject matter of this motion and send it to the appropriate committee. This is only a request of the government to consider. There is certainly nothing compulsory or mandatory with regard to implementing the intent of the motion.
I hope that as the result of this motion the hon. member for Compton and others on the government side will get a message to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) regarding the whole issue of user-pay and the freight rate structure which takes into account our geography and climate in relation to the markets, where goods are produced, and where people want to travel.
The minister issued a press release last February 17 on the Maritime Freight Rates Act and the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act in which he said that the interregional subsidy would be reduced to IVi per cent only until September 1 next year, but there would be a 15 per cent subsidy paid on an agreed list of commodities. These are commodities westbound from the Atlantic provinces and from that part of Quebec south of the St. Lawrence and east of highway 23.
The hon. member sponsoring this resolution wants that boundary moved further west. 1 do not blame him. There are a lot of communities in the townships west highway 23 that have manufactured products and agricultural products, both raw and processed. They would like better access to the markets of central and western Canada. I support that concept. However, you cannot have it both ways.
The government has been saying we must have competition, free enterprise, and profitability in transportation in Canada. With our geography and our thinly scattered population, it does not work that way. My friends in the official opposition have been spouting the same line about profitability and transportation. If you insist on accomplishing that, you will get a reduction in service and a discrimination against producers of agricultural products and manufactured products. This is as a result of where they are located and their access to the major markets.
We support the resolution. We could have an inquiry, but I do not suppose more inquiries are needed. We would like to see a combination of subsidies and/or equalized freight rates applying to a host of commodities which Canadians are very good at producing. However, faced with competition from central Canada and from outside our borders, they are faced with a very difficult problem in the area of transportation costs.
Freight Assistance
It would be more appropriate to select modes of transportation most suitable according to distance and the kind of commodity eligible for subsidy. It is wasteful and inefficient to give subsidies to truck transportation hauling heavy bulk commodities for long distances. It is wasteful and inefficient to give subsidies to railroads for small lot shipments over short distances. If we ever reconcile that problem in transportation costs, not only in the Altantic provinces and eastern towships but all over Canada, we will have a much more equitable distribution of our industrial production in this country, both agricultural and non-agricultural.
In any case we support this resolution. We hope the hon. member's friends will agree with him, unless he is moving his motion solely for local consumption in his own riding and in a couple of ridings around it. I am sure his motives are much higher than that, though. He is serious about this and is anxious to obtain the support of members on his side. I trust the motion will be passed, at which point the hon. member will probably want to enter into serious discussion with his hon. friends, including the hon. member who preceded me in this debate, with the Minister of Transport, and with his parliamentary secretary.

Mr. Speaker, I think each member of the House should meditate on the statements made by my colleague for Compton (Mr. Tessier), in particular when he asks whether our problem is not that the strategies implemented by Canada in regional economic development and job creation, are those of rich towns. We should also meditate the question he put as to whether some people have the right to work when others do not just because they come from remote or less developed regions.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker-and statistics tend to prove it- the government creates every year more jobs than any other industrialized country of the world. As the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) announced it, we know that in 1979-80, the employment strategy of the federal government will amount to $715 million against $420 to $425 million this year.
We also know that between $200 million and $300 million will go to job creation for young people of 18 to 30. However, Mr. Speaker, it can be seen that these programs which in principle are valuable-for instance the employment tax credit which brings much benefit to businesses-cannot be easily implemented in ridings like those of the hon. member for Compton and the hon. member for Charlevoix constituencies where there is no industrial base. The millions of dollars which are being invested through that program will not really help the most disadvantaged areas but will rather have the effect of strengthening the urban industrial base.

Freight Assistance
Extending to the eastern townships the subsidy program which was originally set up for the Atlantic region could benefit the industrial infrastructure of that region. But, Mr. Speaker, a federal-provincial standing committee on transportation matters in Quebec was established four years ago by the Quebec and the Canadian governments. There is a similar committee for Atlantic Canada and another from Ontario and another for the prairies. And this committee's mandate is precisely to make a continuous and permanent review of the efficiency of those assistance programs and make relevant recommendations to concerned political authorities.
Of course, I feel that the issue of freight rates is a major item of any industrial development strategy. That review is already under way, Mr. Speaker, and we will have to make a global review of the whole structure of transport subsidies. And considering the areas whose economic potential is very high and which are very remote, for example the north shore of the St. Lawrence River, and considering the iron ore from the Sept-Iles area we realize that sooner or later the whole north shore of the St. Lawrence will have to be included in an assisted or subsidized area. And in Bill C-20 introduced in the House early in this session, review, Mr. Speaker, which every Canadian province has urged us to make as quickly as possible, I know my colleagues of the opposition are not in full agreement because they want to play politics with those important matters of transportation; they are not too eager to pass Bill C-20 quickly. But, Mr. Speaker, precisely in that bill we tabled in the house, a bill to revise the transport policy, we have enunciated a basic principle, and 1 quote one of the paragraphs of the preamble of that bill, as follows:
3. (1) It is hereby declared that the objective of the transportation policy for Canada is to achieve a transportation system that serves as an effective instrument of support for the achievement of national and regional social and economic development objectives, is efficient and provides accessibility and equity of treatment for users and it is further declared that the objective of the transportation policy for Canada includes the encouragement and promotion of the integration of services employing the most appropriate modes for each service and that it is the responsibility of governments to attend to the provision of the transportation system.
Further on, Mr. Speaker, still concerning the principles of the legislation, it is said that a decision of the government of Canada or of the Government in Canada and one or more provincial governments requires that the achievement of national or regional social and economic development objectives take precedence over the objective of commercial viability.
Mr. Speaker, we are now very far from the scarecrow raised by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) to the effect that the government is committed to the principle of profitability and the "user pay" principle.
Mr. Speaker, hopefully, Bill C-20 will be passed rapidly when the government introduces it in the House. To come back to the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act, I believe we should go back over the history of this legislation to see

why the legislators decided originally in the twenties and again in the sixties to introduce such legislation.
My colleague for South Western Nova (Miss Campbell) has already mentioned these principles, which are quite easy to understand. Following the establishment of the Canadian confederation under the British North America Act, which contained a commitment towards the Atlantic provinces to build a railroad to bring their products to the markets of central Canada, that is Upper and Lower Canada or the regions of Montreal and Toronto, which are the major consuming areas of our country, it was obvious that we had to assist those areas situated far from major Canadian markets through transport subsidies to bring their products to these major consuming centres. A line had to be drawn somewhere, and 1 believe that this was done around 1923 when the Duncan commission established by the Right Hon. Mackenzie King recommended that this line be drawn at Levis and then east of the highway. There was no highway at that time, but centres east of highway 23 were included, I believe, in the review made in 1969.

Mr. Speaker, we have to go back further in time to 1927 and consider first the intention of the legislator of the time, that is when the Maritime Freight Rates Act was adopted in 1927. This act that set up to define the selected territory, the members for Compton (Mr. Tessier) would like to see amended in order to include the eastern townships.
Mr. Speaker, I do not mean to give an unduly long historical background. However we have to go back somewhat in time to determine why the need for this legislation was once felt. As I said earlier, the Maritime Freight Rates Act was adopted following the report of the Duncan Royal Commission of Inquiry which sat in 1926. Among other things, the commission outlined the relationship between some obligations laid down in section 145 of the British North America Act and the situation in the maritimes in 1926. Basically this section provided that the federal government committed itself to building a new railway line linking Halifax to the St. Lawrence. This is how the Intercolonial Railway was built and completed in 1876. You will recall that later, in 1923, it became an integral part of the Canadian National Railways. The Intercolonial Railway was designed to achieve a particular purpose which was to guarantee maritime merchants and manufacturers access to the vast markets of the rest of Canada.
Furthermore, at the outset, approximately from 1876 until 1912 Intercolonial Railway freight rates were maintained to a lower level encouraging exchanges between the maritimes and more crowded regions of central Canada.
But between 1912 and 1927 a succession of hikes in transportation rates reduced the advantageous position of maritime manufacturers. This situation triggered off a wave of vehement protests and discontent in the Atlantic provinces and it was in this context that the then prime minister set up the Duncan commission whose mandate was the following, and I quote:
To undertake a task of national importance in inquiring into the maritime province grievances . . . The commission ... should take every opportunity for the fullest and frankest discussion of the economic difficulties facing this part of the Dominion, the endeavours which have been made to overcome them, the causes of any shortcoming in these endeavours, and the most effective and practicable remedies.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

MEASURE RESPECTING CHARITABLE CORPORATIONS The House resumed consideration of the motion of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand), that Bill S-4, respecting Canadian non-profit corporations, be
2004

December 11, 1978
Non-profit Corporations
read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, prior to the dinner break I was dealing with the bill, primarily in connection with two points. First, I indicated that over the next two years we will see an increase in the number of non-profit corporations, particularly as local communities become more and more involved in activities which heretofore governments looked after; and second, as a consequence of that, we will have to make sure that we are clear on the kind of corporate structures we are crafting to carry out those specific purposes.
Of course it would be wise for us to give uniform consideration to corporate structures, but I do not think we can assume that uniformity will serve our need. It will have to be the kind of structure-and perhaps they might vary from one place to another-to fulfil the needs of the different communities. I might say in passing that when I spoke earlier I had not had the opportunity to read the background paper on the bill, and I note that although the minister's speech came to us, we did not have an opportunity to study it. It seems to me to be always more beneficial and helpful in a debate if we all share the same information.
There are two matters which I should like to touch upon. Although this bill deals primarily and almost wholly with structure and form in relation to non-profit corporations, I do not think one has to be around government very long to recognize that structure and form very often determine content. The first thing I would like to mention is to remind those who are interested in the matter that, as we become more and more involved with non-profit corporations, particularly those dealing with charitable works, we must remember that there is a delicate balance between the operation in connection with government as non-profit corporations carry out those services which the government would normally have to deliver, and the right to participation.
I well remember a matter which was before the House and which was being widely discussed by the public last spring. There was a note from the minister on May 17 in which he indicated that the circular which was put out restricted political participation on the part of those who engaged either in obtaining government grants or were involved in the government in some fashion with respect to non-profit corporations. There was a clarifying statement, which was a good statement, which ended by saying that, according to the courts, political activities are not charitable activities. I appreciate that from the point of view of form and structure, but when form and structure determine content we always run into the difficulty that there is a tendency on the part of government to try to use that form and structure to organize content, and therefore, either inadvertently or with abandon, not worrying, when they should properly be worrying, about the right to political participation by non-profit organizations.
The second area I would like to touch upon is that, as more and more non-profit corporations are established to deal with local needs, we should find a way in which we can make sure
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Ethier).]
that the purposes of those corporations are related to local government.
I do not think members of this House need me to remind them that for a long time municipalities in this country had an enormous difficulty in obtaining funding from the federal government for non-profit corporations to meet local needs. Most of those corporations we are talking about deal with such things as non-profit housing, assistance to the arts, theatre, culture in general, sport, and social services. All of those concern municipalities. As a consequence of having at least three, and sometimes four levels of government which participate financially, I realize it is difficult to organize in such a fashion that it is responsive to local needs. That is the challenge. As we deal with the content of what non-profit corporations will be doing in the fields of housing, art, theatre, sport, social services and other cultural events, it is absolutely essential to realize it is dovetailed and connected with what municipalities do in the country. That is their particular, peculiar responsibility.
Certainly in the last ten years there has been a desire on the part of the federal government to have what has been called the federal presence. I assure the government that federal presence has been known primarily because the government seems to have intruded and to be organizing its affairs in relation to non-profit organizations. Rather than organizing its affairs in relation to the needs of local communities through their municipal councils, the government seems to be acting in defiance of them and confusing them. In relation to the federal government's contribution to local needs stems the provincial government's. Provincial governments have their own concerns. Over the next few years it will be absolutely necessary to work harder in order to ensure that as, the federal government participates, it does so through provincial agreements with municipalities.
If the federal government is looking for a presence by the expenditure of its money, then perhaps it ought to remind itself that it can do so by being known for its good work and not necessarily its advertising. The municipal councils of this country have known too often a federal government which has participated and created confusion. That is something which will be of greater difficulty in the years ahead, as community organizations and non-profit organizations within communities participate in order to serve the needs of communities.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks let me say that we on this side have had a great deal of difficulty compiling information respecting Bill S-4. When we looked around to see what was available, we found the bill. We looked at the committee hearings in the other place from which we gleaned some information. But we lacked an information kit from the department, providing some background information. After a couple of calls to the department, we received at approximately five o'clock a booklet entitled: "Detailed background on the paper for the Canada Non-profit Corporations Bill". I am not cynical enough to
December 11, 1978

believe that this was withheld on purpose, but it says something.
If one wants a good debate in the House, be sure that there is adequate information. If one wants a shoddy debate which will contribute very little to the legislation, dry up the information. Perhaps that is what will happen as we consider this bill. I hope not, because it is an important piece of legislation. It is not something I can become really emotional about, but it is a piece of legislation which has beer, needed for some time.
There are approximately 15,000 non-profit corporations in Canada. Some of them come under federal jurisdiction, approximately 3,000. In the past they have been controlled either under the Canada Business Corporations Act or the Boards of Trade Act. The Canada Business Corporations Act was brought down, put together, debated, and finally passed. The section dealing with non-profit corporations was left out on purpose, because the government felt that non-profit corporations should be dealt with separately. I concur with the government's wisdom in that regard.
Non-profit corporations cover a wide range of activities from health matters to sporting and cultural matters which touch all our lives. The scope and range of volunteer organizations are something which has not been explored adequately. They have the power and ability to react rapidly to situations, far faster than governments. If the bill helps to bring their expertise into focus, then we will have accomplished something.
In the town of Dundas where I lived for approximately 45 years, a young gentleman was set upon by persons unknown and very severely beaten, so much so that he could not work for approximately eight months. No sooner was he out of the hospital and able to go back to work, than his house was burned to the ground by persons unknown. There was a hue and cry to help this man. There was no organization available at the time which could step in and do anything for him. The organizations in the town did not have the funds or structures in place to build him a new house. He had ongoing medical bills which had to be looked after, but no steady job.
The town fathers had a meeting and passed a resolution. They went through the town collecting money, virtually door to door, and received a substantial amount. One thing which hindered them was the fact that they could not say to people donating money that they would be provided with receipts in order to deduct their contributions from their income tax. The reason for that was that the letter sent to the Department of National Revenue was lost somewhere in the maze of mail in the department. In fact I made six or seven telephone calls to the department. To this date I have been told the letter has not been received, even though we know for certain it was mailed. The result of the efforts of the town fathers was very limited. Although some funds were collected to help this individual, certainly it was far short of what could have been done.
Generally speaking, the entire matter of charitable foundations is one which should be examined. I welcome some of the provisions in the bill before us, particularly those which dwell upon the reporting of these foundations. I do not mean to say
Non-profit Corporations
for one moment that there are any instances of fraud. As far as we can ascertain, there has been very little fraud in this field. We can ask anyone in business for the number of organizations requesting donations in the course of a year, and we will see the potential for something going awry. I have experienced this, and like a lot of people in business I received so many requests for assistance that I developed a kind of defence mechanism. Some businesses will put a dollar amount on what they are prepared to give a charitable foundation or a non-profit corporation of one type or another. Others will say, "Write us a letter and we will put it before the committee within our company which will then judge how much we are prepared to give." Others say yes, but when they get off the phone they forget and do not follow through.
We found, as a result of an investigation I undertook with a group of businessmen at one time, that the city where I was doing business was divided into areas and people in fact almost had a franchise to collect funds in those area. No matter what charity was involved, it seemed that different individuals, through some right, and we could never determine just how, collected the funds, and very often the commission rates were as high as 45 per cent.
When I say I welcome the reporting structure contained here, it is because the public donating the funds has a right to know where the funds are going and how they are being dispersed. I might say that the bulk of the sort of thing to which I referred, that is, the general approach to people collecting money on a commission basis, has gone by the boards-at least I hope it has. Nevertheless, that practice was in existence and was very strong over the years.
There have been organized appeals by people who make an outright business of collecting money, and the unfortunate part of it is we do not see very much reporting about where the money actually goes. I think one of the most blatant cases of that in this country took place around World War II times in the form of the "Bundles for Britain" organization across the country. That organization collected millions of dollars, I suppose, and what actually reached the people who needed it amounted to only pennies. The majority of the funds collected was used up on advertising, overhead, travelling expenses to meetings, rallies, and so forth. The actual amount that ended up with the people in Britain who had suffered during World War II was minimal.
We welcome this approach. The ability of charitable foundations to mobilize public interest and gather funds to help research is something of which we are all aware. I have the greatest respect for those who devote their time to the diabetes research group, the heart foundation, the cancer fund, the cystic fibrosis group and other organizations. Those who collect money, including fire departments and various service clubs assist in keeping this research going, with the help of federal and provincial governments. This is a way in which we can express our concern. I know the people in the florist business are unhappy when they see an obituary that says
