something like, forget about the flowers and send a cheque to the heart or cancer foundation, but people like to express their feelings in different ways. Many people I know prefer to send a cheque to one of the worth-while charitable foundations that are contributing tremendously to health research, and we should encourage them.
With this inflow of funds there must be a structure in place to see they are handled properly and meted out to the various research organizations which fulfil the functions set forth in their individual charters. From that point of view this measure is good.
I noted in reading the minutes of the proceedings of the other place that the department has a kit it intends to send out to these charitable organizations which report on an annual basis to the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. The minister would be doing us a favour if he were to see that each member of parliament received one of those kits. In carrying out our duties as members of parliament we come into contact with many of these organizations. If you sent out a questionnaire to members of parliament I am sure you would find that most members are directors, honorary members or patrons of one type or another of charitable foundations. We could do a good deal of missionary work by spreading information about this bill and the requirements various organizations will have to adhere to in coming years.
We note there is a five-year compliance period in the legislation and a further period during which an organization which has slipped by for five years can get back in through an appeal to the governor in council. This is a wise provision and a good way to go about handling the measure. People who work with these charitable foundations, non-profit corporations and membership groups, are usually well-intentioned and well-informed and I would not want to see a club held over their heads. By taking this five-year compliance approach we are allowing them to review their charters, their bylaws and regulations, and a sufficient time to review the legislation in order to determine how it fits in with their organizations. This also gives them an opportunity to amend their constitutions, bylaws, charters, whatever the case may be, in order to comply with the provisions of Bill S-4.
Let me return to the matter regarding information given or not given to us. The preparation of this measure has been going on within the department for a number of years. The department has been trying to get a handle on non-profit corporations for five or six years. As the minister mentioned, the department employed Professor Peter Cumming of the Osgoode Law School to carry out a review. He produced a report, and it would have been very helpful if we had received a copy of that report along with the background detail. This would have given us a much more in-depth idea of what is to be required, and would probably have resulted in faster passage of this measure through the House and the committee.
We have no desire to hold this measure up unnecessarily, but we are at a bit of a disadvantage in that it is to be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. The Christmas break is looming and we have the chairman of that

committee telling us he would like to have this measure considered and reported back to the House before the Christmas holidays on the twenty-first, yet we really do not have adequate information. My colleagues will do their very best to see that this bill moves along at an appropriate pace. If the information is forthcoming it will be passed, but if the information is not made available it likely will not. That is the size of it.
There are many other aspects of this bill on which I could speak. I assume that when we get into non-profit corporations we touch many organizations somewhat international in scope and that many of our Canadian charitable or non-profit corporations are branches or affiliates of organizations in other countries, particularly in the United States.
One of the difficulties facing our department of tourism today is that these organizations are prohibited from coming to Canada to hold conventions, which means a loss of many tourist dollars. Although both countries say that it has nothing to do with the legislation passed that dealt with Time magazine and the closing of the border to American television advertising in Canada, this legislation has caused a good deal of resentment in the United States, and it is one of the reasons that these organizations do not come to Canada. Through an amendment made by the Senate, non-profit corporations and, I suppose, charitable foundations and membership corporations, if they so desire and if I read it correctly, will be allowed to hold their annual meetings outside Canada. I hope that reciprocal regulations will be extended to American non-profit corporations. At least it shows that the government recognizes that there is a fault in this regard.
Another aspect of this bill deals with the closing out of a particular corporation and allowing those three types of organizations to merge. Where there cannot be an equitable agreement on the distribution of any funds remaining, there are provisions for the appropriate organization to apply to the courts to have the distribution made.
We do not make enough use of non-profit organizations and particularly charitable foundations, in this country. Several members of service organizations have spoken to me about this. The president of the Rotary Club in Burlington said to me recently that his club at one time undertook many charitable functions in the course of a year and that it now seemed to him that the government had more or less taken over this sort of activity and did not seem to be too interested in organizations like the Rotary Club, Lions, etc. taking on charitable activities. In my constituency there are many senior citizen accommodations which were made available as a result of the work done by such organizations, and 1 for one would like to see them taking a more active role again.
These organizations can fill the gap and ease the drain on the public purse. They gather together people with tremendous backgrounds. We have to get more of the public and community spirit back into such acts. I may be old-fashioned to say so, but at one time I got a great deal of pleasure out of giving to charity and not getting a receipt for national revenue
December 11, 1978

purposes. I enjoyed imagining someone in the organization saying, "I wonder who gave us $100." I enjoyed this more than the approach we have today when someone says, "Will you give us a donation for so and so? It is tax deductible." I realize that we are working on a larger scale today and things are no longer the way they were, but I think a lot of pleasure and real compassion have gone out of charity giving because of this approach. Perhaps getting some of these service organizations back into the field through legislation will help to change this trend.
If this legislation were to provide a framework and guidelines within which such organizations could work, I am sure the pattern of how they operate would be adopted by the provinces which would in turn probably introduce parallel legislation, if they have not already done so.
I hope the minister will listen to our pleadings about inadequate background information, and that the next time he has a piece of legislation to bring into the House he will remember our pleadings and see that we are adequately informed before we enter debate so that it can move along at a good pace and we can make some progress.

I am not going to speak long in this debate, Mr. Speaker, but I would like to make two or three points which I hope will be useful to the over-all context of the discussion, particularly as the bill goes to committee for more detailed examination. It has struck me that both the debate we are having now with respect to non-profit corporations and the debate we had earlier today on amendments to the Canada Business Corporations Act which, by nature, was primarily a linguistic amendment, more or less hit at the root of the way in which our society operates today.
I can remember hearing a very fascinating speech approximately two years ago, given by a former member of this House and of the present administration, the Hon. Eric Kierans, who talked about the evolution of corporations in the European-North American context, and in which he stated that the whole notion of the corporation and its importance in our society is a relatively recent phenomenon. I would like to talk more about that, because I think it is wise to keep this theory in mind in terms of the major amendment which is before us this evening.
It is important to note at the outset that this particular piece of legislation provides some kind of federal structure for two basic kinds of corporations as defined in the act. As I understand it, we are to have two kinds of membership corporations, one which basically carries on its activities for the benefit of the public, and is therefore defined as a charitable organization, and one which carries on its activities primarily for the benefit of its own members. In either instance these are not commercial enterprises in the true sense of the word. Such corporations-the minister himself has stated that there are some 15,000 of these bodies in existence-are really a recent phenomenon. I do not wish to sound like Methuselah, because when I say recent I am talking about the last century, and in the history of mankind that is not a very long time.
Non-profit Corporations
We have become so accustomed to having these institutions around that we have, by and large, taken them for granted. It is stated very clearly in the background notes for Canadian non-profit corporations that basically the bill is cast as a registration statute. The bill states unequivocally that a corporation has the capacity and also the rights, powers and privileges of a natural person. That, I would contend, is a very interesting phenomenon. In a sense we are providing a more up to date framework for a situation where we are creating an artificial person. That is really what a corporation is under the law. It is the creation of an artificial person for the purposes of certain rights, powers and privileges. It is an artificial person in an ultimate sense that there is no individual person who carries responsibility, liability, or who exercises certain privileges. Because of that fact and phenomenon, in a business sense we have seen evolve in our lifetime a whole new category of "persons" which exercise power in our lives, of a very great magnitude.
In our lifetime it is interesting to note that we have corporations which are much larger than even nations themselves. Some of the largest corporations that exist in the world today,-and I am thinking of corporations of the size, say, of General Motors, or I might even use the description of some of the very large religious bodies that exist that have millions of members,-exist for the purposes of this act as persons within our country, and yet they are not persons. I mean that it is possible for them to make decisions which ultimately affect all our lives without any individual being responsible. To me that is a very great responsibility. It is one that we will have to reflect on at greater length as the years go by.
When I realize the particular definition or responsibility that we are talking about this evening has to do with creating more order and hopefully less government regulation or less discrimination with respect to the operation of non-profit corporations, I am somewhat troubled that we have continued to provide a framework or to provide legitimacy, if you like, for corporate activity in our society without ensuring that it is fundamentally responsible to people.
It is quite one thing to provide a framework for either commercial or non-commercial corporations under national law as we do today, but it is quite another to think of the way in which corporations exist which are not covered under domestic law. Certainly that is increasingly the case with a growing number of transnational corporations. I will not take the time of the House this evening to go on at length about the problems that are being encountered in various United Nations forums in trying to deal with this phenomenon. We have only to deal with the problem that we have in our own situation of trying to ensure adequate disclosure.
I am delighted to see, in this particular legislation we have before us, that there will be much more effective disclosure than is presently the case for non-profit organizations. Although I have not studied it, I would assume that some similar forms of disclosure exist for the Canada Corporations

December 11, 1978
Non-profit Corporations
Act. Perhaps that is something we can explore in committee, or maybe the minister may want to set me straight if I have it wrong with respect to the bill that covers the larger area of commercial legislation, that is, the Canada Business Corporations Act.
I think we must be sure that as corporations, whether commercial or non-profit, receive greater privileges and rights in our society, that that comes with an exercise of greater responsibility. Responsibility must ultimately be in the area of disclosure. The right of the public is to know and to exercise some kind of response when corporations obviously trespass on the basic rights the minister refers to when he talks about this bill ensuring corporations that are registered under it will be operating in harmony with the Bill of Rights. I think that is what he said this afternoon.
That in itself struck me as being interesting. I would like to have heard him speak at greater length about that. However, I am pleased to see that he views this legislation, no matter whether there are 3,000 or 5,000 non-profit corporations registered, as insuring that they will in effect operate in conformity with human rights legislation. I would hope that we might ensure that all federal legislation, in terms of both legislation and regulation, would operate in such fashion, although we know that is not always the case. However, I commend the minister in this instance for ensuring that that framework will exist.
Also I believe it is important, as pointed out in this background document, that, as it says, "The bill requires mandatory financial disclosure by a membership corporation to its members and by a charitable corporation to the public." Here the distinction is made between the two types of non-profit corporations, those that basically serve the membership and those that service a wider constituency. This business of public disclosure, as my colleague, the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) mentioned, is very important. In this day and age when billions of dollars are being raised by charitable organizations, it is important that the general public, as well as the direct membership, be fully assured that these moneys are being raised for legitimate purposes and that the money is being efficiently and responsibly dispensed. So I look forward to the disclosure that is to take place.
May I say that I am particularly concerned about this section because I have attempted to gain, over the last year or two some accurate picture as to the situation in terms of the registration of charitable organizations, as Your Honour is well aware. I have found it most confusing. Perhaps this is because I am not a lawyer and I am unable to understand all of the legal arguments that have been put forward. But as far back as about two years ago, about two ministers, as my colleague from Esquimalt-Saanich says, two ministers of national revenue, I have been trying to find out even the names of those registered as charitable organizations in the country. Quite frankly I have been baffled and I do not think it has ever been properly explained on the floor of this House, and certainly not in any correspondence with me, why it has not been possible for the Department of National Revenue to

make available a simple list of those organizations today that have received a charitable tax number and that are in the position of being able to offer charitable tax status or benefits to those who contribute to them.
In most instances individual organizations which solicit support will tell you whether or not they receive that status. This information is required when filing income tax returns, and yet in requests that I have made on the floor of this House and in correspondence to successive ministers, I have never been given an answer. Usually I am told that it would create some such thing as too much paper work or, in the disclosure of this particular information about the specific names, that somehow or other this would be giving information that would be either damaging, dangerous, or a disservice to these particular organizations. I cannot for the life of me understand the kind of rationalization or lack of response in this area. Therefore I register the mild hope that this particular bill will encourage the new Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Abbott) to be forthcoming on this matter.
I think this is a basic right of the people and taxpayers of this country, to know on an annual basis, if you like, those that are registered for purposes of charitable donations. If anything it will be one form of insurance where an individual may- because we have had cases of fraudulent situations reassure himself that the organization he is giving money to at a specific point in time has been registered, or has been registered for a period of years, if he wants to know that there is some continuity of likelihood of that organization being able to carry on and fulfil the objectives set forth in the pursuit of its particular program.
I look forward quite optimistically to having a more regular statement. I do not want to know in a detailed way each and every charitable organization's activities, or the disbursement of its funds. I presume that information will be available to those who want to inquire directly of a specific organization. As I understand it, that will be the law. I do think it is not beyond the range of responsibility and possibility of a government to provide an annual list.
Certainly I will press for that to take place on a regular basis.
There is something else about which I am concerned. This will come as no surprise to members of this House. I refer to the way in which the government treated charitable organizations when they began to raise issues embarrassing or disturbing to the government. This goes back over two or three years.
I recall the first instance when this became an issue. It was about two years ago. A particular religious group was demonstrating about the rights of certain people who were being discriminated against in the Soviet Union because of their religious views. In that instance, a particular group in Canada was advertising that it was going to demonstrate in front of the Soviet Embassy. When officials in Revenue Canada heard that this organization was going to carry on a demonstration against the Soviet Embassy because of what was happening to
December 11, 1978

some of their confreres in the same religious group in the Soviet Union, Revenue Canada suggested in conversations with this group they would not get their charitable status renewed. Apparently they had suspended it for a period of time and it was not going to be renewed if that group participated in that kind of political activity. There was quite a row raised on the floor of this House about that kind of intimidation. The threat was then withdrawn.
Less than two years later a more recent minister of national revenue issued a set of guidelines, so called, that were circulated to all groups which had this charitable tax status, listing the kinds of proper and improper activity which they could engage in, a kind of setting forth of the guidelines for acceptable political activity.
Putting it the other way, any group that engaged in political activity would, according to the definition of Revenue Canada, soon lose its charitable number. Again this whole position was based on the flimsiest kinds of grounds.
First, it was based on a couple of court cases that were certainly not recent and which showed very little relevance to the present situation. The interpretation that was put on these cases went, from my point of view, away beyond what those particular cases in effect decided. I thought it entered very much into the situation of departmental officials, if not ministers, beginning to intimidate or to some degree limit the freedom of action of charitable organizations of this country. From the number of groups I heard from-church groups, service clubs, voluntary organizations of one kind or another-[DOT] this did not go down well. It did have the effect of raising some very real fears among these groups as to whether the government might be able to cut off their charitable tax status. We still have not resolved that issue. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said, the government finally suspended or withdrew the particular memo. However, he very much implied in the answers he gave in this House that the basis on which those regulations were set out still stood. There has been no substantial clarification or clearing of the air on this very contentious matter.
We are left in a real dilemma as to what are the criteria, the acceptable role if you like, of charitable organizations. We are also left with the question of who really decides what those criteria should be. Unfortunately, the danger still exists in terms of the kinds of intimidation that can occur, even in this legislation.
On the first page of the background papers, there is this intriguing and somewhat disturbing statement, and I quote:
-the bill, although it applies specifically to non-profit corporations seeks to achieve the same general goals as does the CBCA; that is, to set out a legal system that is clear, comprehensive, and practical:-
No one will disagree with that.
-to minimize the scope of the administrative discretion exercised by department officials;-
That is to be commended. Here is the important part:
-to relegate to the regulations the detailed rules, particularly the financial disclosure rules; and to simplify all statutory formalities with a view to increasing operational efficiency in the respective offices of the corporations,-
Non-profit Corporations
It is still implied very clearly that there will be a section for regulations or, as it states, detailed rules, not just the ones having to do with financial disclosure but perhaps other interpretations that some zealous official might put on what is a properly constituted activity of a non-profit organization in the charitable field.
It is becoming increasingly clear that we must have a good airing of this matter. We must have a thorough public examination of the role of charitable organizations in our society today. The more I have thought about this whole debate and the issue of contention that has existed here with successive ministers of national revenue and their officials, the more I have become concerned about some of the attitudes or philosophic assumptions on which some of this debate has been based.
There has been almost an automatic assumption that somehow or other the activity of charitable organizations and political issues are mutually and totally exclusive of one another. Quite frankly, that is extremely superficial. If one thinks about the very nature of charitable organizations, the reason for which a great many of them are brought into existence, one realizes in many instances they have been brought into existence to deal with issues with which the government or elected authorities have not come to terms.
Certainly most of the major social changes and improvements with regard to governmental responsibility over the lives of people very often began with voluntary associations or charitable groups. If we think of improvements in the situation with respect to people's housing, the provision of various social services, the whole issue of medical care and health services, many of these began with groups and associations that were purely in the charitable field.
Yes, and anti-slavery.

And anti-slavery, as the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) reminds me. Many began in a voluntary way. It was only a few years down the road that governments decided to exercise their responsibility on behalf of all of society.
If a very strict interpretation had been put on this from the beginning, if at the outset officials had narrowly defined the issue of political activity as that famous circular did earlier this year, where would we be now in terms of responsive and responsible society? We would be in a very sorry state. That is why I am quite alarmed and very much concerned that a government minister or an official would think that somehow or other we could separate this into the kind of watertight compartments envisioned in that regulation.
If a charitable organization is being responsible, it will from time to time likely be involved in issues, sometimes of controversy, and sometimes of criticism of those in positions of authority. If we are going to have a narrow definition, if we are going to have regulations that prohibit the expression of opinion, even to lobbying from time to time on specific issues, we will not only do a disservice to charitable organizations and

December 11, 1978
Non-profit Corporations
the basis on which they exist today, but we will do a major disservice to ourselves and our society.
Therefore, I simply argue at this point in the context of this bill that we not begin to envision regulations or begin to have narrowing definitions that really take the life, heart and some of the purpose out of what has been of primary importance in the activities of charitable organizations. As the minister knows, there are only 45,000 to 50,000 of these, and only a small number are registered for these purposes under this kind of legislation. Many would never seek nor in fact need this kind of national registration. What happens, of course, is that the major ones come under this kind of law. Therefore, any change they make will set the style, pace, and direction which many of the others will follow.
I hope in committee there will be more opportunity to explore this area. It is of very great concern, particularly having seen the many instances in the last year or so when officials who are either overly sensitive or overly narrow in their definition, or simply not realistic, impose the kinds of restrictions that do nothing but harm to voluntary and charitable activity in our country.

Mr. Speaker, this may not be the occasion of a very exciting debate but I should like to register the opinion that some very important things have been said by all those who have taken part in this discussion. That goes for the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand) and for all my friends to the right who have spoken.
I should like to underline some of the things which have been said, and perhaps add two or three words. First, may I refer to the comments which have just been made by the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) about the relationship between work done by voluntary, non-profit organizations and the services which are provided by the state through various agencies. I subscribe to the views he has expressed in that connection. I go on to say, as I have done many times in the House, that the thing of which I am most proud about the public life of this country in the last few decades is the fact that we have greatly improved the services which are available to our people. Those services include not only maintenance of income but a whole range of health programs which are available through the various health centres. I think of areas such as rehabilitation and assistance to handicapped people in many ways. There just is no comparison between what was available two or three decades ago and what is available now. However, I did not rise to make that speech-members have heard it made a few times before.
I simply want to say that as one who is most excited about the gains we have made in the public sector, I join with all those who have spoken in saying that a very important sector in our society is occupied by voluntary and non-profit organizations. The hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kem-pling) mentioned some of them, and other organizations have also been mentioned. I think of groups that work with crippled

people, associations which are interested in paraplegics or multiple sclerosis patients.
We all know our own constituencies best, and in my own constituency I think of organizations like the Ellen Douglass Association which works with the staff and teachers of the Ellen Douglass School caring for crippled and handicapped, children. I think, too, of the work done by the Manitoba Association for Crippled Children and Adults. Such organizations do a tremendous amount of good work. They are pioneering in efforts the state may yet take over, and they are doing a tremendous service. They deserve recognition. They deserve this bill-I wonder whether many members have gone right through it to determine whether its substance matches its volume.
I think of various groups working with youth, with women, with boys and girls. There was an organization known, not long ago, as the Boys Clubs of Canada; in keeping with the times it has become the Boys and Girls Clubs of Canada. Then there are the veterans organizations. Today, a number of them work not only with veterans, disabled and otherwise, but are branching out to render services to civilians who suffer from disabilities of which they have experience. War Amputations of Canada is an outstanding example of this. And, of course, there is the Sir Arthur Pearson Association for the War Blinded.
We do well to take these few minutes today to pay tribute to the voluntary organizations, the non-profit groups that do this kind of work. I know that when I visit a place like the Ellen Douglass School in my own constituency I am impressed not only by the kind of service which is given but by the patience and the warm, human touch of those who teach and care for these disabled and handicapped persons. They deserve whatever praise it is to have their work mentioned in the House of Commons.
Having joined in that rhetoric-it is part of this debate and I regard it as important rhetoric-I want to support as strongly as I can one other theme which has been mentioned by previous speakers. The theme I wish to support has to do with the income tax regulations. I listened with interest to the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth saying it used to be more exciting to give for the sake of giving than to give because you get an income tax rebate. But today that is part of the way in which our society works, and many organizations of a voluntary character depend upon the contributions they are able to get because income tax deductibility is available to those who make those contributions.
I found it quite disturbing a year or so ago when the Department of National Revenue put out guidelines or a circular which seemed to warn some of these voluntary organizations that they had better not get mixed up with anything which might sound to the department as if it were political, or that they had better not be critical or caught saying anything which might be embarrassing to the government, if they wanted to keep their tax status. Surely, groups of people who are working for the good of their fellow human beings on a voluntary basis ought not to be looked upon with suspicion by
December 11, 1978

the government as though they were trying to get income tax deductions they did not deserve. I am not satisfied that the matter has been fully straightened out even yet. The previous minister did not get it straightened out in this chamber, nor did he do so in the other chamber. And since then he has lost that job. Of course, members of the other place go on and on-
For ever.

Not really. They are only allowed to go on until they reach the age of 75. Fortunately, that is not the case in this chamber. At any rate, I am glad two or three hon. members have made this point tonight and I hope the government will take it seriously.
There is one other thing I want to say. I find it rather strange that the government should have brought in this bill at the very time we have learned that as part of the program of cutbacks the Department of Supply and Services has instructed its publications centre to cut down drastically the amount of government informational material it makes available to libraries generally, and to university libraries in particular.
Like many other hon. members around here I have been waiting for several days to participate in the question period in connection with this matter. When one waits several days and does not get into the question period, he falls back on Standing Order 43. That is why I moved the motion under Standing Order 43 I did today to make the point. I am sorry that the new Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. De Bane) was not here to hear my motion, but I shall see that he knows about the proceedings both this afternoon and this evening. For a government which is talking about wanting people to have greater access to government documents and government publications to be cutting down on the extent to which it is prepared to make those publications available to the libraries of this country, and to be imposing particular restrictions on university libraries, I think is a very sad mistake.
It is perfectly true that we are getting letters about this matter. I am glad we are, and I hope the letters are coming not only to us who are private members in this House but also to the government. I know that every time we stand up in this House and say "This is a cutback which ought not to be made," the government says, "Well, we have to cut somewhere." Mind you, the government cannot say to us the things it says to my friends to my right as to which way they are going. We just happen to think that involving government in the life of this country is an important way to advance the cause of civilization. We do not advance the cause of civilization when we cut back on the material which is made available both to libraries which are open to the general public and to our university libraries.
I hope that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, who is here for this debate and who, I hope, is following it, will take that message to his colleague, the new Minister of Supply and Services. I understand that some of the
Non-profit Corporations
ministers who have taken over departments they did not have before are wrestling a bit with some of the decisions they are expected to implement. I hope the Minister of Supply and Services will see fit to reverse the decision about supplying government publications to libraries generally, and to university libraries in particular.
Those are the few thoughts I wanted to add to this discussion. This debate may not reach the crescendo of excitement we sometimes get around here, but I believe we are talking about something which is very important in Canadian life.

Mr. Speaker, remembering the remarks which have just been made by my friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), to the effect that we are talking about something important this evening, I am frequently puzzled by the priorities assigned by this government to the legislation it brings before this House. I just happened to look at Friday's Hansard, and I noticed on page 1941 that the order of business as set forth by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) was, first, Bill S-4, legislation respecting non-profit corporations, and then Bill S-5, Canada Business Corporations Act amendments. The order in which we have dealt with those two bills today has been reversed. Then came Bill C-13, amendments to the Electricity Inspection Act and the Gas Inspection Act. Then came legislation dealing with the Canada-France trade agreement, which is facetiously described as the champagne bill. In the present state of Canada's economy these are considered by this government to be the bits of legislation we should be studying.
True, we have dealt with a number of quite important bills since we came back here in October. We have dealt with the family allowances bill, the old age security bill, and the unemployment insurance bill. Some of these bills have gone through, and some are still in committee. We dealt with a borrowing authority bill. The government had to backtrack on that one. It had to move back from $17 billion to $7 billion. It had to lop off $10 billion because it could not tell us where it was going to spend it.
This afternoon and this evening we have been dealing with two bills, Bill S-4 and Bill S-5, which by their dimensions at least are important. The bill we are considering now is 150 pages in length and contains 242 provisions. I would like to come back to that in a moment. However, as I say, I am puzzled by the priorities this government set for its legislation. Where, for example, are measures which would deal with the key problems of unemployment, inflation, and business uncertainty, which are facing our country today? Where are the ways and means provisions which flow from the budget? Where are the changes to the Income Tax Act which are required? Where are the changes in the excise tax law and in the customs tariff law which are required? We are still waiting for them. The country is waiting for them. Business is waiting for them.
We have before us Bill S-4 and Bill S-5, which set up elaborate paraphernalia and structures to create and to put
2012

Non-profit Corporations
corporations in place, be they non-profit corporations or otherwise.
I did not have an opportunity to be present at the hearings regarding this bill which took place in the Senate. We learned on Friday last that this bill was to be before us today. I have not had a chance to see what representations were made to the Senate by non-profit organizations, about their concerns regarding the complexities of the structures which are set out.
I wonder if those who drafted this legislation ever considered such small charitable or non-profit organizations-a huts non-lucratifs, as it is aptly put in the French language-as the organization which is set up to ensure that the leg-hold trap will be abolished in Canada. That is a small group. It gathers dollars and fifty cent pieces from school children and adults all over Canada, but in order to quality as a non-profit organization this group has to subscribe to this bill comprising 150 pages and 242 clauses. This organization will have to have a lawyer. It will have to pay subscription for lawyer's fees in order to make sure that they are operating within the law. It seems to me that a non-profit organization is a nonprofit organization is a non-profit organization. I cannot see why we have to use 150 pages to define one. There are some- they are specified separately here-which have a somewhat different nature. I refer to chambers of commerce and the like, but what about voting powers, proxies, and that sort of thing? I am sure those provisions are not needed for all non-profit organizations in Canada.
My friend, the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald), mentioned the number of non-profit or charitable organizations there are. I recall putting a question on the order paper about three or four years ago. I received an answer saying that there would be so much work involved in producing this kind of information that it would not be economically feasible. As my friend was speaking, it occurred to me that there is one way of doing this. There must be a list somewhere, there must be a list in Revenue Canada, otherwise there would not be a little X, Y, Z number. Maybe they have the SIN too, I am not sure. If they do not have one, they can invent one, as my colleague, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) said, because that is the new system. If you do not have one, you invent one and you proceed in that way.
There must be a list of the organizations which are given the right to issue receipts for income tax purposes. Where is it? I would say it is with Revenue Canada. Why is it not available? Why is there not just a copy of it available? Let us have just one copy in the Library of Parliament. That is one place where it could be. I see no reason why it should not be there. It must be a public document. Those of us who want it or need it would then know whether this or that organization was entitled to issue receipts for income tax purposes, and because of the inter-library loan system, that document would be available for consultation in any library in Canada. Thank goodness we do have that inter-library loan system. I think if there were specific titles of groups mentioned on the list, they could be

looked up in the copy which would be in the library and, I suggest, in the Public Archives of Canada. It could be changed from time to time, but there is a loose-leaf system for making amendments to government regulations.
I wonder whether there is a swimming pool incorporated, for example, that is on a charitable organization's list so that those who build swimming pools for prominent people can obtain their income tax deductions that way.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Be more specific.
I do not think there is any need to be any more specific. What I have in mind is fairly evident.
Take the plunge.

I will take a dive at it.
I am also a little concerned about the matter which was raised by the hon. member for Egmont. He stole some of my thunder, but I think it is worth going over the matter again. I can remember when, in the month of May this year, those regulations came out and the furor that was raised about what they meant, about who was going to bite the bullet and who was going to continue engaging in the activities in which they had been involved. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that there was an information circular dated February 27, 1978, No. 3. I think it is worth putting it on the record in part. It reads:
The purpose of this circular is to explain to registered charities and to charities seeking registration the consequences of having objects and carrying on activities that are political in nature.
I well remember that my friend, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, raised the question on May 1 and 1 raised the question on May 3, and during two or three weeks in May the government was balancing from one foot to the other, saying that the circular was not really an instruction but was merely an accumulation of the jurisprudence on this matter. There is no jurisprudence in this document. These are threats, plain threats.
Then, toward the end of the discussion in the House- because I do not think the discussion is fully ended since this was left very vague-the Prime Minister said in a pet, "All right, I will rescind it for you, if that is what you want." Do you rescind information circulars? Surely you can cancel them. I do not think rescinding was quite the word to use. You can withdraw them, which I think would have been the proper word to use. Rescinding has a somewhat different meaning. I have not looked it up recently in the dictionary, but it does not bear quite the same meaning of permanence that cancellation or withdrawal has, to my way of thinking.
I should like to go on and cite one other piece from this information circular. The second paragraph begins:
It is well established at law that an organization whose purpose is the attainment of a political object is not organized for a charitable purpose.
When the hon. member for Egmont was listing some of the activities of organizations, I mentioned the anti-slavery organi-
December 11, 1978

zation in the eighteenth century. What about the organization to change the penal laws in the nineteenth century? That was political acitivity. They did not get deductions for income tax purposes in those days, I am sure of that. But today there is the John Howard Society and the Elizabeth Fry Society. These societies are formed for the sole purpose of making sure that the penal system of this country is run in a humanitarian way, and when there are any regulations or any pieces of the law which, in their view, do not correspond to their definition of what is humanitarian, they are not mute and, God bless them, they should not be. They should stand on their hind legs and scream, and they should not be penalized for it either. The same applies, as I was saying, to those who are showing their opposition to the leghold trap. They became involved in political activities; they wrote to their members of parliament. It says here in the circular, "An object normally is said to be 'political' if its ultimate intention is to influence the policy making process." It speaks here about writing to members of parliament and so on.
I find that sort of circular issued to organizations which are fulfilling a very important role in our society an abomination. They are fulfilling a role that no government in any democratic country will ever be able to fulfil or should fulfil. These channels should be open to our citizens to express themselves, and to influence legislation and legislators. This particular information circular is an abomination. When we were asking these questions we could not say too much in our preambles, but "abomination" is the only word I can think of to describe that document. I would like to think that it will be definitely withdrawn, as in some other unfortunate incidents in which this government has been involved.
That is a long list too.

Yes, it might cover even more pages than this bill covers. I think that this particular information bulletin might go along with many others.
As I mentioned, I was rather staggered to see the size and complexity of this bill and the detail into which it has gone for the proper constitution of organizations that are designed to fulfil charitable purposes or of those who wish to come together on a voluntary basis to further a legitimate social cause. I do not know why they have to go any further than that-that is a simple definition, I should think. I suppose it could be refined a little more. But I do not see the necessity of going to this length to define that type of organization.
The booklet outlining the detailed background of this particular bill is a fair number of pages in length and is in fine print. At page 11 it reads as follows:
As a result, the bill, although it applies specifically to non-profit corporations, seeks to achieve the same general goals as does the Canada Business Corporations Act-
Non-profit Corporations
It continues:
-to relegate to the regulations the detailed rules, particularly the financial disclosure rules; and to simplify all statutory formalities-
Goodness gracious, there are 150 pages of detailed description, and there will be regulations in addition to that. How will associations out to ban the leghold trap fit into that system? How will those seeking amendments to the Criminal Code or other federal statutes, such as those affecting the gun laws, fit into that system? They have a legitimate right to stand up, complain, and make a corporate joint approach to government on pieces of legislation to which they object. They want to be within the law. They do not like the law as it is, and they want to see it changed. What about those concerned with the death penalty, prison reform, and abortion?
This bill is 150 pages long and contains 242 clauses, in addition to regulations. It defies the imagination of one who feels we ought to be thinking in simpler terms about our legislation and not in more detailed terms. I doubt that people with causes to further will be able to get from the beginning to the end of this bill without going to sleep. They will go to sleep and not understand more than the first two or three pages, if that. Yet, they will have to subscribe to it.
Therefore, among the comments the minister will make as he closes this debate, I hope he will address himself particularly to the status of this information bulletin. It is not a bulletin which emanated from his department. It belongs to the Department of National Revenue. If he does not make some comment about it, I am sure the matter will be brought up again in committee. That dreadful document should disappear because it is a shadow over all charitable organizations. They want to know exactly where they stand and where it stands with regard to them. If the minister is not able to say anything about that particular regulation, I hope he prevails upon the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Abbott) to come before the committee and make the appropriate statement.

speakeroldname: Miss Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words before the minister closes the debate. Bill S-4 is a very weighty tome respecting Canadian non-profit organizations. Supposedly it will have the effect of lessening the possibility that moneys donated to and expended by charitable organizations and membership corporations will not be used for the purposes for which they were intended, and that occurrences of abuse or fraudulent behaviour will be reduced.
The bill is a vehicle to expedite the work of the volunteer sector of our society. For that reason I applaud its objectives. But sometimes I think that we would do a lot more to encourage volunteers if a bill of this complexity could be written in plain English so that those to whom it applies would find it more comprehensible. As it stands, probably it necessitates the services of a corporate lawyer for days and even weeks to read, understand, and transmit its intricacies to the voluntary sector.
Because I have a very healthy respect for what volunteer organizations contribute to our society, and because I have a
