Non-profit Corporations
belief that they could do even more if they were not so hampered by bureaucratic red tape, I attempted to plough my way through this particular bill to see if it made reference to a matter which has been raised on a number of occasions this evening. It is a matter in which I am particularly interested and which I and others have raised in the House on a number of occasions. I am referring to the information circular which was noted by the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) and the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro).
This circular was issued by Revenue Canada last spring. It dealt with charitable organizations and political activity. But search as I would through the 242 clauses of the bill, I could find no reference to that particular aspect of the role of volunteer organizations. One might say this is not surprising, since the matter should more rightly be dealt with by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Abbott) or the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). That is true after a fashion, but since the government has promised for many years to do something about updating the rules and regulations concerning the activities of volunteer organizations, particularly as they pertain to disclosure, I thought possibly this bill would be used for the purposes of clarification. I am referring to clarification as far as the guidelines of last spring were concerned. Those guidelines issued by Revenue Canada, far from recognizing the contemporary role of volunteer and charitable organizations, had the effect of restricting their activities considerably.
When I stopped to consider this promise by the government to attempt to make the rules and regulations covering charitable organizations more applicable to contemporary society, I found I had to go back eight years, to the time when the promise was first made in the budget speech of Edgar Benson. At that time, in 1970, he said that a review of the tax laws, as they relate to charitable organizations, would be undertaken. As far as I can find out, that is when the promise was first made. But in 1977 the government's advisory council on volunteerism recommended a series of measures to safeguard citizen groups from political pressures. Even that more recent advice to the government has not been heeded.
Did the government consider proceeding with reform of outdated rules and regulations? Did it consider getting on with the work of clarifying these vague laws? No, that was not the manner in which the government proceeded. It did not decide to clarify and set out what could be considered contemporary legislation regarding charitable organizations. Instead, last April it circulated to charitable organizations across Canada this circular 78-3.
As has been stated by my colleagues, this circular warned churches and charities that they risked losing their tax exempt status if they engaged in so-called political activity. Political activity was defined in the circular as any activity that has as its objective the changing of any legislation or even the maintenance of existing legislation. It included seeking support for their objectives from members of parliament or from the general public by means of the media. That may have been
acceptable to the then minister of national revenue, and it may have been acceptable to his colleague, but to those of us on this side of the House, sir, not only did that approach seem to be very punitive, it also had the effect, as far as we were concerned, of stultifying rather than encouraging the work of the volunteer sector of our society.
At that time an editorial in the Toronto Star responded to the activities of the government and to the circular put forward with regard to charitable organizations. In that editorial of April 18 it referred to the way in which the Trudeau government was trying to muzzle volunteer organizations. It said:
This is outrageous. It's based on National Revenue's interpretation of a body of law that goes back to Britain 300 years ago and which takes the narrow view that while charities can directly aid the needy, for example, they can't advocate changes in public policy that might benefit the needy.
It pointed out the incongruity of that approach.
As a result of that there was a series of questions asked in the House by a number of us on this side, members who were very concerned that this particular circular represented a very dangerous intrusion into the democratic right of free speech. At that time questions were raised in the House, in the committee, and during exchanges between this chamber and the other place where the minister was then sitting, and he replied to my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) by a letter, explaining that the charitable status of organizations "would not be prejudiced by limited attempts to promote the interests of those organizations at the political level". At this point the minister introduced a new note to the discussion for debate. This issue became compounded by that of limits or the lack of limits of ministerial discretion.
I asked the minister at that time in what way he was able to sit in judgment on the activities of churches or charities, as to whether their attempts or interests should be limited in any way and, if so, how he would define those limits and where he got his authority to do so.
As has been noted, under heavy attack in this House the government finally agreed to withdraw the circular. The victory was a very uncertain one, because government spokesmen insisted that they would continue to enforce the law according to their interpretation of it, circular or no circular. As a result of that, Canada's charitable organizations were left with the threat hanging over them, that if they did not conform and if they did not curtail their political activities, they might face punitive action by Revenue Canada. That, of course, is what happened, and has happened on a number of occasions since.
When I look back over my records I find it was on May 3, the then minister of national revenue wrote to inform me that he had decided to withdraw circular 78-3, for review by his officials. Having received that kind of communication from the minister, one might have gathered that the intimidation which was connotated in the circular would also have been withdrawn. Yet, sir, on June 11 of this year it came to light that a women's group, the Brampton Women's Centre, had been forced to sign a statement that it would take no part in

December 11, 1978

political activities if it were to receive or qualify for its standing as a charitable organization and receive charitable status for purposes of tax deductions. The president of that particular group admitted she had signed only under pressure, because without the charitable status that was to be accorded her organization, the organization would not be able to continue or exist. I ask you, sir, is this an example of government action which is directed at promoting voluntary activity in our society?
At that time I referred to the incident regarding the Brampton Women's Centre as a danger to our entire political system, and a failure to keep a promise to redraft the circular. A little over a month after the minister had assured me that the bulletin was being withdrawn and reviewed, his department was proceeding to threaten organizations such as this one, the Brampton Women's Centre, because it was felt that they would engage in political activity of a nature relating to women's interests. It strikes me as rather ironic, sir, that if Agnes MacPhail and Nellie McClung, in their fight for women's rights in this country, had been forced to withdraw from their activities by governments of the day under that kind of intimidation, probably I would not be in a position to stand in the House of Commons this evening.
As a result of that incident regarding the Brampton Women's Centre questions were raised in the House of Commons as to the intent of the government in respect of volunteer organizations. Once again I heard from the then minister of national revenue. Having promised that the circular would be withdrawn for review and clarification, he apologetically explained to me that what was involved was a specific paragraph in the Income Tax Act, and that he had no authority to withdraw that. He went on to include this paragraph in his letter of May 24:
It may well be that the legislation is too restrictive ... that it has not kept up with the time. For that reason I have asked my colleague, Hon. Jean Chretien, Minister of Finance, to review the applicable provisions of the Income Tax Act. Meanwhile, however, my officials must administer the act in accordance with its present provisions. I assure you, nevertheless, that the department's practice is not to be unduly restrictive with charities.
What kind of language is that with regard to charitable organizations in this country?
Earlier I mentioned correspondence which I had from the minister that referred to limiting attempts of charitable organizations. Subsequently he wrote that he would not be unduly restrictive regarding charitable organizations. How can we assure that charitable organizations in this country will carry out work on a voluntary basis, work that we desire them to carry on, if they are to be threatened, or their activities curtailed by implication that the government will not be unduly restrictive? What does this really mean? What does it mean?
We have already seen in the case of the Brampton Women's Centre that they would not have received their funding had they not given a commitment that they would not take part in any political expression. How many other organizations across
Non-profit Corporations
Canada since that time have received similar threats or have been similarly intimidated, and about which we do not know? How many charitable organizations which might have been functioning, refused to place themselves in a situation where they felt that their freedom of speech was being curtailed or their activities limited? How much of this has gone on of which we are unaware?
There are some things we do know for certain. We know that the Department of National Revenue has not yet got around to involving voluntary organizations in any redrafting of circular 78-3, or even to seeking their opinions on redefining what their role should be in the 1980s and the 1990s. It is a very different role from that of the 1930s or the 1950s and whatever prehistoric legislation upon which the government bases its circular 78-3. We know that the Minister of Finance has not got around to revising the restrictive clauses of the Income Tax Act which curtail the activities of voluntary organizations very significantly at the present time.
I note in this Bill S-4 that a non-profit charitable organization will still have to apply to the Department of National Revenue for a number in order to qualify for tax deductible status. In this bill we are presented with rules and regulations as to the number of directors, the meetings of these directors, the practices of quorum, the use of proxy, the role of the auditor. How much better this bill could have been had the minister urged his colleague, the Minister of Finance, or the Minister of National Revenue, or both of them, to do what Mr. Benson promised in this House eight years ago, to review and to update the tax laws as they relate to charitable organizations so that no one would feel pressured or intimidated, and no charitable activities would be restricted or organizations' work curtailed by the heavy handed government interfering with the true goals of voluntary activity in our society. I hope that the minister takes that message to his colleagues.

A person should not have to speak on a bill like this, Mr. Speaker, but sometimes it becomes necessary because of the very poor drafting. We have here some 150 pages, plus another number of pages with schedules, which mean absolutely nothing to the ordinary person who actually makes up the majority of memberships of non-profit and charitable organizations in this country. Its purpose is to set up another bureaucratic empire for this government to take further taxes from this country.
Bill S-4 is for the formulation of the Canada Non-Profits Corporations Act. Nowhere in the definition section, however, is the word non-profit defined. It seems to me that if we are going to have an act with 150 pages defining what it is, at least the word non-profit should be clearly defined. The definition for charitable organizations is very general, and upon reading other parts of this bill I wonder what is the real principle. I believe that the real principle behind the bill is to set up another bureaucracy to take away the powers of voluntary or service club organizations. Nowhere in the definition section are the words "religion" or "philanthropic", words which are used in most non-profit corporation acts in our country. It is

December 11, 1978
Adjournment Debate
just another empire or bureaucracy, with more taxes and waste.
I wonder, too, if this bill, S-4, is really inter vires this House of Commons. It came from the Senate, but does its object really come within the powers of this parliament? It may for raising money, but that is not what it purports to be, an act to provide for the incorporation of charities or non-profit corporations.
What of those companies which have already been incorporated by provincial statute? Many of the non-profit, charitable and voluntary organizations across this country have in fact been incorporated under provincial statute, under a reasonably fair set-up, with little cost to them for set-up, and with very few forms to fill out. With this bill an organization will have to hire not just a plain lawyer to incorporate but a Philadelphia lawyer to decipher it.
As one reads through this bill, clause after clause, the general principles are, "as prescribed by legislation or as the ministry decides," but then that happens all the time in this House.
Shall I call it ten o'clock?
Mr. Speaker, could the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of Privy Council tell us what the bill of fare is for tomorrow?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, tomorrow we will be dealing with Bill C-9, an act respecting public referendums in Canada on questions relating to the Constitution of Canada.
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 40 deemed to have been moved.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to place on the record some of my concerns as a result of a response made to a question I posed to the Minister of Communications (Mrs. Sauve) last December 1. I might say at the outset that my concern does not rest on the competence or the sincerity of the parliamentary secretary, but rather with the spirit of the response, which I do not think adequately replies to the concerns which I dealt with at that time.

What has happened is that in metropolitan Toronto an organization called Rogers Cable Television has been presenting on their community cable channel the House of Commons question period live each day, and, as well, on one of their upper band channels reached by a converter they have been playing question period and, I believe, some other House of Commons programming. The regulations of the CRTC say that when a company has House of Commons programming on an available channel other than the so-called community channel, then you should not use the community channel for House of Commons programming. I termed this situation, in my original question, as regulation wise, common sense foolish.
In the course of a conversation on other matters a few weeks ago between an officer of Rogers Cable Television and an officer of the CRTC, the question was posed by Rogers as to whether there was any difficulty, because of existing regulations, with their playing question period live on that regular community channel which is readily available to anyone with cable television in the Rogers subscribing area. It was indicated in that conversation, as I understand it, that if a company had House of Commons material on another available channel, then it should not, according to that regulation, be broadcasting it on a community channel. Perhaps the principle behind the regulation is to prevent interference with community channel programming. It is a very wise-sounding and equitable regulation. The problem is that not all cable subscribers have converters, and thus in one fell swoop, a result of that interpretation and that telephone call, Rogers Cable felt it would be wise not to be in contravention and withdrew question period from their community channel.
I understand from a conversation with someone from Rogers Cable this afternoon that they have 200,000 units in homes in Toronto. They have sold about 30,000 converter units to some of those homes. Another 30,000 people have rented units, for a total of 60,000 out of 200,000, which would leave 140,000 homes, not people-there are many more people-who all of a sudden because of that regulation wise, common sense foolish decision no longer had available to them the proceedings of the House of Commons of Canada, the focal point of activities at the federal level. To me this seems to be an absurd development.
It may well be there are fewer than 140,000 people lost this service, because one could purchase a converter in any store. But, at best, at least half of those people, or 100,000 homes in Toronto, could receive question period live until a week or so ago. Today they cannot. Surely if we want people to understand better the operations of government and the concerns expressed by representatives from various parts of our country, that kind of silliness is unnecessary.
I understand there are very serious negotiations under way with regard to bringing the proceedings of the House of Commons to Canadians across the country, and I gather this problem will be resolved in the not too distant future. I do appreciate the principle that one channel on the main band
December 11, 1978

using cable is intended for community programming. I also understand there were no serious disruptions and that the few changes that were made to accommodate question period on that community channel via Rogers Cable in Toronto were made with no difficulty and no complaints. Meanwhile, I argue further, what could be more important or considered of more, community interest than the proceedings of this House, especially daily focal point which makes evident what is troubling people across Canada, what the points of confrontation are, and the differences among the various parties?
I know that my hon. friend, the parliamentary secretary, being a wise and reasonable man and a former broadcaster, who represents a great community, one of the most beautiful areas of Canada, one well known to me, will probably say in a moment or two that this silly business has been resolved.
If he does not, I will forgive him, but I count on him, because of my confidence in his ability, to go back and urge his minister to address this issue to the CRTC. Hopefully we can have a good common sense resolution and bring back the proceedings during the question period to at least those 100,000 homes in Toronto, a good many of which are in my constituency.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. Douglas (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly want to thank the hon. member for York West (Mr. Fleming) for the kind things he said. I wish I could give him a more complete assurance than I am able to tonight concerning the problem he has put before the House. I must be quite honest, however, and tell him that according to the information I have received the problem has not been solved up to this point. But I am sure the CRTC, knowing the importance of broadcasting proceedings of the House of Commons to all citizens of Canada, not only to those in the city of Toronto and in the riding of York West, will be endeavouring as early as possible, as is the committee of the House of Commons itself concerned with the broadcasting of the proceedings, to provide the citizens of Canada with the best coverage of the House that is available.
One of the prime considerations we have to look at is the definition of a community channel. The purpose of a community channel is to represent and involve the community in a particular licensed area. The hon. member for York West made the eloquent plea that broadcasting of the proceedings of the House of Commons, in particular the question period, in that prime area would be of community interest. I agree that the happenings here in the House of Commons are of community interest to a large majority of the population, but is it community programming? We can probably get into quite a debate on that.
The view put forth by the CRTC is that it must involve participation of the people of the community that it serves to qualify as community programming.

What about the MP?
Adjournment Debate

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
The hon. member asks about the MP. We would be making quite an exception to the rule, not only in the city of Toronto but all across the country. We must realize there are areas outside the city of Toronto that are unable to receive the types of programming and broadcasting, particularly the cable service, which is available to viewers in that fine city on the shore of Lake Ontario.
I believe, because of the participatory role, the community itself should contribute to programming on the community channel. Therefore in this case, with a few members of the House of Commons, most of them from Ontario, the proceedings of the House do not fall within the parameters laid down by the CRTC as community programming. While the House proceedings do, without question, have a wide community interest, they clearly do not and cannot be construed as Toronto programming.
I do not say that broadcasting of the House proceedings should not have wide national distribution. I would put forth the idea that proceedings of parliament should be available to as many Canadians as possible. One way of achieving that would be to make the question period available as part of the national broadcasting service through the CBC. This would mean that approximately 98 per cent of all Canadians, not just those in Toronto, would receive the question period, which, as the hon. member said, involves members all across this country. The full proceedings of the House could then be carried over cable, but not on the community channel.
This is a very fine definition. I do not believe the community channel is the answer to providing wider access to the broadcasting of proceedings of this House. It should and must be done through our national broadcasting system.

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-JET SERVICE TO WESTERN MANITOBA AND EASTERN SASKATCHEWAN
AIR TRANSPORT-JET SERVICE TO WESTERN MANITOBA AND EASTERN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to deal tonight with the perennial subject of air service to western Manitoba and eastern Saskatchewan. I do so because it has become critical. The Canada Winter Games open in Brandon on February 12. Air service is essential to the success of the games.
There have been repeated promises that air service would be available. However, the way things are proceeding at the moment, we will not have the required air service. Let me repeat the promises that have been made over a long period of time. On May 23, 1974, on a special trip to Winnipeg during the election campaign, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced as follows:
The undertaking I am announcing on behalf of the government is as follows: we have asked Air Canada to work with each provincial government to determine what action is necessary to put in place in each province a third-level air carrier system that will provide high quality local air service, promote industry, reduce isolation and provide jobs. Air Canada will then co-operate with the existing carriers in each province to put in place this service. Air Canada will if necessary, either directly or through a subsidiary, provide that service.
Later in the statement the Prime Minister was more specific, and I quote:

December 11, 1978
Adjournment Debate
In another area of air service, air policy, industrial development and job creation, I would like to announce the following: approval in principle has been given by the government for the provision of air services linking Winnipeg, Brandon, Dauphin, Yorkton and Saskatoon as a test of possible new third level air policies, the ones I talked about earlier. This will be air services linking these western cities.
That is a definite promise-an election promise, it is true, but election promises should be fulfilled.
After a series of questions in the House and after various delays, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), in a news release dated January 31,	1977, made the following
announcement:
The government will make contributions to operating deficits not exceeding the amounts indicated below for either jet and/or non-jet type services over the following possible routes: for jet services Regina-Brandon-Toronto, $1.1 million ... for non-jet services, Winnipeg-Yorkton-Saskatoon, $.5 million-
This is another specific promise made by the Minister of Transport. Transair, the regional carrier, applied to provide these services. They were taken over by Pacific Western Airlines. Great Lakes Airlines applied for the rights that would be abandoned by Transair and made an offer to buy out Nordair so that it would have sufficient equipment. Instead of agreeing to the proposal of Great Lakes Airlines, which is a reasonable regional carrier in this part of Canada, the ATC not only denied the sale but the government itself decided to buy Nordair. This was described by Mr. Geoffrey Stevens in the Globe and Mail of November 8 as "a weird decision". He wrote:
Its the weirdest decision to come out of the Government of Canada in many, many moons. Just as the airline industry was losing hope that the cabinet would ever make up its mind. Transport Minister Otto Lang announced late yersterday afternoon that the cabinet had reached a decision on Air Canada's proposed purchase of Montreal-based Nordair.
Well, we were back to square one, because Nordair refused to provide air service to the western Manitoba and eastern Saskatchewan area which represents a population of some
200,000.	They are willing to provide jet service to Dryden, Ontario, but not this important area of western Manitoba and eastern Saskatchewan.
I was in touch with the Minister of Transport and he explained that, in these circumstances, there seemed to be no financially practical way of providing Brandon with air service to the east and west, desirable though that would be. This was in a letter dated October 11, 1978. Yet in the House the other day, in reply to a question by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), the minister came up with a new theory. He stated:
I continue to support the right and wisdom of ministers making judgments on the basis of social needs as well as economic needs and I am glad to stand here and say so on behalf of my predecessors and myself.
Later, he added:
It is also my impression that I fully answered the hon. member and told him why it is that sometimes, on a non-economic basis, a minister will make decisions and recommend situations to government on the basis of what is good for a province, region or development, not necessarily justified on economics alone. I said that and I said it very fully.
That contradicts the response he made to me that western Manitoba could not be provided with jet service on the grounds that it was not economically feasible.
The minister has received petitions from large numbers of people. The government of Manitoba has made a special appeal to the federal cabinet. The deadline for making a decision on these matters is almost due with respect to the winter games, and I urge the Minister of Transport-I am sorry he is not with us tonight for this important discussion- to authorize Air Canada to provide this service. Air Canada flies over the area several times a day. The only difficulty is that it is hard to reach it at an altitude of 30,000 feet. Air Canada is the one carrier which is now able to provide this service. In 1974 the Prime Minister promised that Air Canada would be authorized, if necessary, to provide this service, and I trust that whoever speaks for the government in reply on this matter will indicate that there will be air service in time for the winter games, which commence on February 12 of next year.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Lapointe (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-JET SERVICE TO WESTERN MANITOBA AND EASTERN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is still some misunderstanding surrounding the matter of the provision of jet service to western Manitoba and eastern Saskatchewan on time for the opening of the Canada Games in Brandon in February. I would like to take the opportunity to try to shed some light on that matter.
It is already established that the airlines decided themselves not to provide that service to Brandon or Yorkton after the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) invited them to do so. It should be specified immediately that no airline made a request to provide a jet service to Yorkton and that only Transair made such a request for Brandon but withdrew it afterwards.
It has also been suggested that if Great Lakes were now the owner of Nordair they would provide that service to Brandon. I feel there is nothing less sure. Great Lakes, as all other carriers asked to submit an application, have reviewed the financial implications of a service to Brandon and have found that they would incur very heavy financial losses. It should not be concluded that the possibility of a jet service to those locations has been definitely discarded. The air carriers have considered the service and have merely decided that at present it would not be profitable. In addition, if the carriers find that the demand for an air service is sufficient, they could then submit an application to the Canadian Transport Commission to obtain the necessary permit.
I am sure that my colleagues know that the Minister of Transport cannot ask Air Canada to provide that service to Brandon as long as a regional carrier cannot do so, as requested by the hon. member, even if Air Canada aircraft fly over that area several times a day. I should point out that in such a case it is proper to let airlines decide what services they will
[Mr. Dinsdaie.j
December 11, 1978

provide and file an application with the Canadian Transport Commission.

I think that the government lived up to its promise when it announced financial assistance for Prairie Air Services on January 31, 1977 and provided for a contribution of up to $1.1 million for jet service between Regina, Brandon and Toronto, and a contribution of up to $0.9 million for jet services between Winnipeg, Yorkton and Saskatoon. I have already stated that the result of this effort was that no carrier applied to service Yorkton, and only one offered to service Brandon, an offer which was later withdrawn.
The Minister of Transport has had continuing discussions with the airlines to encourage some interest on their part in coming forward with an application. The government has done all it could on the matter to this time. The carriers have indicated that this service to western cities would be a non-economic venture at this time unless a greater demand could be shown.
The Minister of Transport still stands ready to provide whatever help is required to make that kind of application work.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH AND SAFETY OF WORKERS EXPOSED TO ASBESTOS HAZARDS
LABOUR CONDITIONS-OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH AND SAFETY OF WORKERS EXPOSED TO ASBESTOS HAZARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 23 I addressed a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), who is responsible for protecting and maintaining the health of Canadians. At that time I asked the minister to investigate claims arising from a U.S. court case that Canadian asbestos companies were aware of the potentially fatal health hazards to which their employees were exposed but that these companies took no action to inform their workers.
In fact, one of the documents introduced in the case against the asbestos giant, Johns-Manville, indicated that although the company took steps to warn Americans of the asbestos danger as early as in 1964, it did not do the same in Canada until 1968.
It is a sad fact that thousands of Canadian workers may have had their lives put in jeopardy because information regarding asbestos dangers was suppressed. I asked the minister to look into the matter and to discuss with the provinces what action might be necessary. The minister expressed some reluctance to do this. She stated that she did not want to create "unnecessary panic in the public", and those are her exact words. I also do not wish to create panic, but it is certainly time to express more concern than the government has demonstrated so far.
I am not so much interested this time in assessing individual corporate guilt or innocence in this matter, although that certainly bears further investigation. For the most part, the
Adjournment Debate
damage has been done, but I am interested in determining what is being done for the victims, or for those who will soon be recognized as victims, since asbestos-related diseases usually strike 20 to 30 years after exposure. In the United States, the health secretary has already warned that as many as half of the workers who worked with asbestos during and after the second world war might be afflicted with lung cancer or other asbestos related diseases, such as asbestosis. Some medical experts are worried that we may soon have an epidemic of asbestos-related diseases on our hands.
Only this morning it was reported that five workers who were employed during the Second World War in a Defence Research Board plant which processed asbestos filled gas masks have died as a result of a disease associated with exposure to asbestos. Others who worked in this plant are undoubtedly at risk.
Clearly it is now incumbent upon the government to set up procedures to identify all the employees of its wartime defence plants who suffered similar exposure to asbestos. It must be determined if they have developed asbestos-related diseases and, if so, they and their families must be compensated for the suffering involved. The government should set an example for the asbestos companies, if the companies themselves refuse to take any action. This would be one small step in the right direction.
There is now sufficient medical evidence, and a sufficient number of cases have been made public, to suggest that immediate action should be taken to determine how many Canadians have been affected, and what can be done to assist them. To this end, it is imperative that the Department of Labour's new Centre of Occupational Health and Safety enter into discussions with the provinces and develop a co-ordinated plan of action.
When I made this suggestion to the then acting minister of labour last month, he informed me that there have indeed been consultations on this subject. I would like to ask the new minister or his parliamentary secretary what was the result of those consultations. Were they aimed at determining what persons have been affected, what medical attention is appropriate, or what government involvement will be required.
This problem has been ignored by the government and by the asbestos companies for far too long. It has developed into a series of horror stories of hardship and suffering on the part of innocent people who worked in the asbestos industries, ten, 15, 20 and 30 years ago, not knowing that they were constantly exposing themselves to health hazards. I feel it is only fitting, as a result of what we have found subsequently-and indeed there have been some asbestos-related diseases that were discovered and documented as early as 1903 and during the 1920s, 1930s and 1940s-and that it is incumbent upon the federal government, in concert with the provincial governments, where asbestos companies are operating, to provide ways and means, financial if necessary, for the victims of asbestos-related diseases not to go the compensation route, which is not nearly enough, but to provide them with financial assistance, where necessary, in order to bring civil actions in a

December 11, 1978
Adjournment Debate
court of law, against the companies if the companies refuse to compensate them themselves.
It has been proven that companies have been derelict in their duty to inform workers or personnel concerning the dangers of working close to asbestos, and therefore exposing themselves to asbestos-related diseases. If the companies refused to inform the workers, then the workers should have the right to sue their employers if they have contacted asbestos-related diseases, which are practically always terminal in nature. If workers died as a result of exposure to asbestos, then their children and wives should have the right to sue the companies. Workmen's compensation is simply a cheap way for companies to get off the hook and put it back on taxpayers, government funds, and contributions made by the companies to workmen's compensation.
I ask the government to take action on this and to provide financial means where necessary, so that these persons who have contacted asbestos-related diseases from working in asbestos mines, even if they have been retired for several years, will be able to bring actions in a civil court of law against their employers or former employers.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dennis Dawson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH AND SAFETY OF WORKERS EXPOSED TO ASBESTOS HAZARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 23 the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn) asked the now Minister of Public Works (Mr. Ouellet) if discussions were taking place between the provinces and the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety concerning the health effects of asbestos on persons working with or exposed to it.
The act authorizing the establishment of this new centre was proclaimed on October 1. Since then further action has been taken to bring it into operation at an early date. Members of the governing council of the centre, drawn from labour, management, and provincial and federal departments, are in the
process of being appointed. The inaugural meeting of the council is being planned for mid-January.
I appreciate the concern of the hon. member regarding this serious occupational hazard. I know his concern is shared by many members in the House. Certainly I will bring this question to the attention of the council for its early consideration. However, I should mention that in 1975 the Department of National Health and Welfare completed a study of asbestos in the work place. It recommended that all jurisdictions adopt a more stringent standard, namely, two fibres per cubic metre. This reduction of exposure limits from five fibres to two fibres was promptly made applicable to all industries operating under federal jurisdiction and subject to the dangerous substances regulations pursuant to part IV of the Canada Labour Code. I understand a number of the provinces have taken the same action.
The seriousness and complexity of this hazard, both in its occupational and environmental aspects, are widely recognized, nationally and internationally. It is my hope that the centre, by fostering collaboration among all jurisdictions and facilitating joint action, can bring about real progress in providing more effective protection to those whose work exposes them to asbestos in its various forms and usages.
Also I am aware of the recent report of health problems of employees of the defence research plant which made mask languid asbestos. The Department of Labour will investigate this situation. We will attempt to identify any persons whose health has been adversely affected by virtue of this contact with asbestos. We are prepared to apply provisions of the Government Employees Compensation Act if appropriate. I will inform the hon. member later with more specifics.
